Whether Jews should be tolerated in the society of Christians? The horrendous judgments of God exercised upon the Jews on account of their ingratitude and incredulity were not only set forth long ago in the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, the slaughter of the whole nation and the destruction of the Mosaic Polity: but they also remain before our eyes to this very day. For we see them living dispersed among all nations throughout almost the entire world, subject to the empires of others hard and unjust, to be objects of contempt and scorn to all, and to be treated no otherwise than as slaves or chattels, as much by Christians as by Mahometans and other infidels: finally, not to be received by some and to be expelled by others who had already received them and tolerated them for a long time: in some places, they even barely redeem passage or safe conduct through provinces for the sake of making a journey with a great sum of money. Certainly, in previous centuries, they were excluded from all of France at once and together, no less than the Templars. Similarly, they are exiled from all of Britain. Rupert the Elder, Count Palatine, for I know not what reason, expelled the Jews not only from Heidelberg, but also from the entire Palatinate: and he donated their synagogue, which has now been converted into a Medical Auditorium, and most of the buildings to the Academy, which he founded not long after. And it is known what has been plotted against them in these recent years, partly in Frankfurt, partly in Worms. Nor are there lacking specious reasons by which it is usually persuaded that they are not to be tolerated: They are, they say, enemies of God and Christ, blasphemers. They are enemies of Christians, usurers, money-lenders, who afflict and suck dry the poor. They are also traitors who betray the secrets of Christians to the Turks and others of this kind. On the contrary, there are also found those who undertake the patronage of the Jews, and either tolerate them or receive them anew, or even persuade that they ought to be received and tolerated: but some are led by the hope of profit or gain which they receive from the Jews: others are impelled by a zeal for charity and their conversion. Therefore, so that it may be clear what ought to be decided or followed here, I shall submit an explanation of the problem constructed from the Word of God. I premise, however, two theorems, necessary to be observed. One, that the Jews ought to be considered by us in four ways. They are to be viewed: I. as men, participants of the same flesh and blood as we are, and sprung from the same parent, Adam. II. as descendants of Abraham, as the firstborn of the family of God. In which respect the apostle does not hesitate to call the Jews of his time, although senseless, rebellious and unbelieving, nevertheless ‘saints’: by reason of the fathers, that is, of the firstfruits and the root, from which the lump and the branches are considered sanctified. (Rom. 9:3-5; 11:16) III. as enemies of Christ and the true Church, blasphemers, infidels, money-lenders, usurers: for which reasons they are the offscourings [καθάρματα] of the world, and the public hatred of the whole orb.

IV. That they are to be converted to the faith of Christ, according to the grace of predestination and the promise of the eternal Covenant, initiated with Abraham: and indeed [they are to be converted] in great number and multitude. Which conversion, as a mystery divinely revealed to him, the apostle proposes in Rom. 11, verse 25 and following, and confirms it clearly, partly by reasons, partly by the testimonies of the prophets. The other point: That those four modes of consideration ought to be viewed by us not separately, or individually one by one, but all of them conjunctively. When therefore it is asked, whether the Jews are to be tolerated among Christians, one must not judge separately from the third mode, in which they are said to be enemies of Christ, infidels, usurers, but one must pronounce simultaneously also from the others, and especially from the second and fourth: in which they are called the seed of Abraham, to be converted to Christ and to be brought back to the society of the Covenant. This is the reason: because the apostle speaks and judges of them in that way and no other. Rom. 11, verse 16, ‘For if the firstfruits are holy, the lump is also holy; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.’ Likewise verse 28: ‘they are enemies for your sake, but beloved for the sake of the fathers.’ According to these things we now answer affirmatively: namely, that the Jews are to be tolerated in the society of Christians. These are the reasons: First: Although God imposed upon them the punishment of dispersion, so that without a king, scepter and civil law they live scattered among other nations throughout almost the whole world: yet He preserves them wonderfully, nay even miraculously, so that they are not destroyed, nor can they be destroyed, although it has been attempted by many: nor are they even confounded with other nations, in rites, ceremonies, marriages, and the custom of their whole life. And as Cain was marked divinely with a sign, lest he should be killed by those he met on account of fratricide: so the Jews seem to be marked by God on their faces and foreheads, on account of the slaughter of Christ the firstborn, so that they can be recognized almost at first glance, lest they be killed. Therefore, those who do not wish to tolerate the Jews seem to oppose the counsel of God. Second: The dispersion of the Jews throughout the Christian world is useful to us Christians: and that in two ways:

I. On account of the spectacle of the severity and wrath of God, which ought to be kept perpetually before our eyes. For they are shown to us as branches broken off on account of unbelief, so that through faith we may learn to remain in the true olive tree, Rom. 11:22 ff.

II. On account of the testimony of sound doctrine, which they carry about in the Scriptures of the O.T.: so that the Church may everywhere find witnesses of the Christian religion, as Augustine teaches, Of the City of God, bk. 18, ch. 46. And this testimony is so much the firmer because it is borne to the doctrine by the very enemies, and indeed sworn ones, of it. Therefore the fathers called the Jews the librarians of the Christians, enemies in their hearts, witnesses in their books. Hence, lest we be an obstacle to ourselves, we ought to bear with the Jews in our society. Third, from the examples of the apostles: Peter and Paul showed the highest charity to those very Jews who had driven the Lord Jesus to the cross although they had heard his doctrine with their own ears and had beheld his miracles with their own eyes; and who, having corrupted the witnesses of his glorious resurrection with money, were even much more detestable than the Jews of today; and they did not hesitate to seek and procure their conversion by all means, even at the expense of their own safety: so far were they from being unwilling to tolerate them, Acts 2-3; Rom. 9. Therefore it is much more fitting for us to do the same regarding the Jews of today. Fourth: The Jews, according to the doctrine of the apostle, Rom. 11, are again to be converted to Christ and to faith in Him. But since this cannot be done by infidels, who themselves are ignorant of Christ and do not receive Him, but must be done by the ministry of Christians and the faithful, they certainly ought to dwell and converse among them. Fifth: The Apostle teaches that not only are the Jews to be converted in the greatest number, but also the manner of conversion: which he establishes in this, that they be provoked to emulation, Rom. 11:11, that is, that by the example of the faithful from the gentiles, they themselves also may desire and embrace the grace of Christ. If the Jews are to be provoked to emulation by us, by our example, they certainly ought to be tolerated by us and to dwell among us. From this, however, we further gather two things:

I. That the Jews ought to dwell among Evangelicals and Orthodox rather than among Papists. Reason: because the latter are less fit to excite emulation in them: since they are idolaters, whom they [the Jews] turn away from and execrate with their whole heart.

II. That conversion of all Israel, or of the Jews in the greatest number, of which the apostle prophesies in Rom. 11, will without doubt follow immediately upon the ruin of the Papacy, and the destruction of the city of Rome, since Papism is the chief obstacle and greatest impediment to the conversion of the Jews to Christianity, which they almost measure by that idolatrous Papism. Sixth. If all Christian magistrates were to exclude the Jews from the society of Christians, and would no longer tolerate them; they would certainly have to be relegated to the Garamantes and Indians, to the Caribs and Cannibals, so that they might spend their lives among them. But in that way, it would surely be poorly provided for them regarding teachers, who might show them the way to find the Messiah whom they seek. We conclude, therefore, that the Jews are to be tolerated among Christians. Furthermore, since it is acknowledged that the Jews, according to the third consideration are not only infidels, but also blasphemers against Christ, enemies of Christians, and most iniquitous usurers, their toleration must be circumscribed by certain conditions as if by certain laws. Here, therefore, some things must be avoided and shunned by Christian magistrates, and other things, on the contrary, must be done: Those things must be avoided which, on account of usury and participation in it, [countries] either admit or tolerate Jews—which, alas, is excessively common today in Germany and elsewhere. Furthermore, these things must be done and cared for by Christian magistrates:

I. That the Jews in their synagogues and sacred assemblies should only read the Holy books of the Old Testament and call upon the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob according to the Scripture of the Old Testament.

II. That they should take care that they be instructed in the Christian religion and taught about it: indeed, that they even compel them to attend the sacred sermons of the Christians from time to time. For otherwise they can neither be provoked to emulation nor converted to the faith of Christ. And the neglect of this admonition is perhaps the primary reason why so few Jews are converted today.

III. That they also accustom and lead them to honest labors and honest crafts: so that they may thus be able to sustain life honestly, even without usury.

IV. That they provide them with the security and defense due to all citizens living according to the Laws: and that they do not allow them to be vexed with impunity by the injuries of private individuals, whether publicly or privately. Which is also, alas, too much in use! It is, however, against the apostle, who gravely forbids us Christians from injuries, insults and contempt of the Jews.

V. That they ensure that the Jews are distinguished from Christians by their dress or by some certain sign, so that no one through ignorance may associate with them just as they would with Christians. In sum, Christian princes and magistrates who have received or are receiving Jews into their protection, shall show, both in these and in all other things, that they are moved to that [protection] by nothing other than holy charity and a desire to procure their salvation: and therefore they will permit them nothing that is in itself illicit: they will take care that they be instructed in the Christian faith and truth: so that they may thus be able to be salutary instruments in that work which God promised He would do through the prophet Isaiah and the apostle Paul. This much concerning the problem itself.

Amongst Gregory’s Epistles, there is one De Judaeis non persequendis [That the Jews are not to be persecuted].) He says it is a perplex[ed] question by reason of the different judgments. He propounds: First, diverse arguments of those which hold they are altogether to be cast out of a Christian commonwealth by reason of those horrible blasphemies which daily, both in their ordinary prayers and in their speeches they belch out against Christ, the Virgin Mary, our Faith, and all Christians in general, and for other reasons which he there alleges. Secondly, He urges other arguments to prove that the Jews are not to be cast out, but tolerated under the Christian magistrate, because by that means many of them may be converted by continual converse with the Christians, and the Scripture seems evidently to confirm that, Hos. 3:4; Zeph. 3:7; Lk. 21:24; Rom. 11:25-26, and because they may be serviceable to them against the pagans and for other reasons. He himself goes the middle way and lays down his opinion in certain propositions: First, It is better for Jews to live amongst Christians than under Turks or infidels. Secondly, The blasphemies of Jews are not to be tolerated, but to be prohibited and most severely punished by Christians. Thirdly, the Jews are to be esteemed among Christians as the servants of servants, that is so to be handled that they are exiles and cast off by God Himself. They are not to have any public office. They are not to practice that unjust usury for which they are so infamous amongst Christians. They are to have also (said he) some outward mark in their garments, by which they may be distinguished from others, and [are] to be forced to hear sermons. Many other cautions does he give in the receiving of them. As for the toleration of the Jews, whosoever they be that suffer the exercise of their religion with the blasphemies they commonly use against Christ, make themselves guilty of all their wickedness, which the Lord keep this land from, as well as from the abomination of the Mass. The Pope can tolerate the blasphemy of the Jews and the filthiness of all the courtesans and stews, and take a yearly rent of them for it, and for no respect will allow the exercise of our most holy religion either in his own dominions or wheresoever he may prevail against us. t: §17. Now to the Political Means. I. Nothing is accomplished, indeed, things are done badly, by persecuting, harassing or oppressing the Jews, driving them away, or killing them. That is to say, those guilty of Judaism alone [should not be harassed or oppressed]. But those guilty of other crimes should be punished equally with others. Nevertheless, they should not be treated more harshly for that reason, because they are Jews. We do not wish innocent people to be constrained merely because they are Jews or Saracens. Among the ancient Sicilian laws, Emperor Frederick established this in Constitutions of Sicily, bk. 1, title 17 & 26: ‘We cannot allow Jews and Saracens, whom the diversity of the Christian sect makes hostile, and who are deprived of every other assistance, to be defrauded of the power of our protection.’ Christian converts from Judaism have noted that this perverse practice of treating Jews more harshly is a great hindrance to the conversion of more people. For it is entirely foreign to the nature of faith to employ violence in order to produce belief. Petrus Alphonsus the Spaniard, in The Dialogue of Moses & Peter: ‘To imprison and kill, until someone either believes or pays a tax, is not among the works of God; nor did any of the prophets command anyone to be compelled to believe.’ Likewise, Stephanus Isaacus (to whom, together with his father Johannes Isaacus, Cardinal and Papal Legate Franciscus de Mendoza had granted authority to investigate all the Jews throughout the three ecclesiastical electorates, and to rage against them with fire and sword) rightly said that this counsel was unjust and most wicked, and that more is accomplished through moderation and kindness than through cruelty or savagery, in his German Apology, p. 42. The same was noted by [Johannes] Pfefferkorn [d. 1523] and others. Therefore, the better and more common opinion, both among theologians and among jurists, is that the Jews should be tolerated—not indeed enticed, but, where they are found, not treated more harshly. Thus: • Baldus, vol. 1, Consil, 315-16 • Rolandus a Valle, vol. 3, Consil, 25 • Alexander of Hales, Summa, pt. 2, Questions 179-80 • Vincent of Beauvais, Spec. t: Must so many efforts be used to force from us [French protestants] that French heart that God and birth has given us? What have we done to merit so many misfortunes and such severe punishments? We are hunted, we are drove up and down as if we were the plagues of the Republic; We are treated as the enemies of the Christian name. In places where the Jews are tolerated, they have all manner of liberty, they exercise arts and merchandise; they are physicians, they are consulted, the health and life of Christians is put into their hands: And as for us, as if we were infected, we are forbidden to approach children that come into the world, we are banished from the bars and faculties, we are removed from the king’s person, we are banished from societies, our charges are taken from us, we are forbidden the use of all means that might secure us from being famished; we are abandoned to the hatred of the people, we are deprived of that precious liberty that we had purchased by so many services; our children are taken from us, who are a part of ourselves; we are made to lead a languishing life, in lowness, in poverty, and often in dark prisons. Formerly, when declarations were made against us, they were at most contented with registering them in the rolls. They are at present fixed up, they are cried about the streets as if they were gazettes, to inspire the people with a spirit of fury against us. And they have been so successful that in the great cities of France we expect to have our throats cut, one time or another, by a popular sedition; so that we are very near the Inquisition. Can it be said that there is liberty of conscience in a kingdom where the people are banished, lose their honor, and their goods are confiscated for religion’s sake? There needs nothing more than fire; and that terrible tribunal of the Inquisition, which France has been hitherto so much afraid of, will be established there. Are we Turks, are we infidels? We believe in Jesus Christ, we believe him the eternal Son of God, we invoke him solely; and we have no idols. We have a sovereign respect for the sacred Scriptures, we believe there is a Heaven and a Hell, the maxims of our morality are of so great a purity, that they dare not contradict them. We have a respect for kings, we are good subjects, good citizens, faithful in commerce: Let us be tried according to law, and it will appear if we have been engaged in any conspiracy against the State, and if we have any ways failed in our duty. Thanks be to God, nothing can stagger our fidelity, and the stock of love we have for our prince is not to be drained: if it depended on our enemies, we should be enemies of the State we make a part of; they design to push us on to crimes, that the king may have a just occasion of ruining us; but they have hitherto missed their aim, and are like to do so still; the king may see it, whilst that they so successfully turn the effects of his goodness from us, there is not one of us but who is ready to lose his life for his sake; we are Frenchmen as well as we are Reformed Christians; we would shed to the very last drop of the blood of our veins to serve our king, and for the preserving our religion, even to death.

t:
Question 9, Whether Jews in a Christian magistracy are to be tolerated, and how are they to be dealt with? There are extreme opinions concerning this question. The first sentence is of those who absolutely deny that Jews ought to be at all tolerated in a Christian commonwealth. The moments of their assertion they advance are these: (1) Jews are extremely blasphemous; for at the name of Jesus, if they alone be present, thy cry out and say: “Let his name be blotted out”; they call the Holy Trinity nonsense and foolishness, they call Christ a spurious one; they call Mary, the blessed mother of the Savior, dung; they curse every Christian magistrate, they reckon Christians among the most lost and damned men; they think it lawful to despoil and kill Christians and treat Christian rites as obscene. (2) They think Christians to be plainly objects of hatred and enemies to God; they bring accusations against secular and principal Christian commonwealths and so separate themselves. The second judgment, plainly contrary to the first, proposes causes of hope and arguments and proofs of foundations: (3) From those things themselves is Christ made according to the flesh, Rom. 9:2, 5. A corrupt religion is extremely blasphemous: to be possessed of the habitation of the Jews within the commonwealth yields very many benefits to Christians: for they show spectacles and thereby furnish a divine mirror against the contemners of the Gospel, and they can serve for the restoration of the integrity of the monuments of the Old Testament, and confirm the truth among the images of divine predictions, Rom. 1:22. They enrich the commonwealth with money, with trade, they make it opulent and wealthy. (4) The ejection of the Jews out of the republic would carry with it many inconveniences: for being utterly expelled from Christian dominions they are more difficult to be converted and more free to blaspheme, and the Turkish kingdom would be augmented by their resources. (5) It is necessary therefore that Jews live somewhere, if any political use proper to them be by them entirely prescribed: wherefore it is preferable that they live under a Christian magistracy, as under which the hope of a more abundant conversion would shine forth than that living under a gentile magistracy they either persevere in their idolatry or pass over to the blasphemy of the gentiles. The third opinion is intermediate, since it concedes indeed that Jews may be tolerated in a Christian republic, but under certain cautions and conditions. In these conditions to be prescribed, the sentiment is not the same of the Pontiffs and the Lutheran doctors. Becanus the Jesuit, in the Manual of Controversies, bk. 3, ch. 18, pp. 728–29, 1–3, etc., embraces by three conclusions the opinion of the Pontiffs. The summary of the dissertation is that the magistrate can permit the vices and exercises of the Jews if there be a sufficient cause; that the magistrate can also permit usages of theirs, if sufficient cause be known; that the Christian magistrate cannot in good conscience permit, nor leave unpunished the external hatred of the Jews toward Christians. The Lutherans, however, concede to Jews dwelling in a Christian republic under other cautions and conditions, namely:

1. That a free exercise of religion be not conceded to them: circumcision is forbidden to them: polygamy is not permitted.

2. Blasphemy is to be punished in them very severely and restrained by most grave punishments.

3. No public office is to be entrusted to them.

4. That that monstrous usury, by which they drive Christians out, be not permitted.

5. That they be compelled to attend Christian sacred assemblies.

6. That care be taken lest they lead Christians away to the Jewish religion. Which and similar conditions and cautions about tolerating Jews in a Christian republic are required by: D. Helvicus in his System of Judaical Controversies, list of Jews 8, or the last; D. Hutterus in L.C., article 32.9.6, p. 1,037. Dn. D. Gerhardus, tome. 6, thesis 223 of Common Places, article on the Political Magistrate, pp. 890–91 ff., and the theologians of the Jena Academy in their counsel on this matter in the year 1611, and the Theological Faculty of the Academy of Frankfurt on the Oder in the year 1613, reported by Dedekennus, vol. 2, pt. 2, p. 139 ff. & 146 ff. Those conditions were conceived and prescribed piously and prudently, yet they are such that they are more easily desired than obtained. For who indeed could obtain this from the Jews, that they refrain from blasphemies against Christ and from unjust and biting usuries? For if they do not blaspheme Christ openly, yet privately they do not cease to be vexatious with shameful dealings. And he takes away a Jew’s life who prohibits usury to him; for he cannot do without it any more than he can do without common air. But how grave a sin it is to draw the yoke with unbelievers, or to grant them hospitality and the right of citizenship, since they hold a doctrine different from the doctrine of Christ, is more evident from the Scriptures than to require proof. Therefore Luther also, in Disput. Fratr., 8, in Epist., fol. 94 ff., judges with more deliberation concerning the Jews.

t: Question 8, Is it lawful to tolerate the synagogues of the Jews, in which they blaspheme the name of Jesus? Although there is no lack of rescripts of civil and canon law by which synagogues are permitted to the Jews, and it is granted that they should neither be killed, nor violated, nor hindered in their festivals (L. nullus, et L. die, Sabbathi, C. de Judæis, l.6; C. de paganis; see also the sanction of Theodoric, King of the Romans, in Goldast. Regis, apud Goldast., vol. 3 and of Emperor Conrad IV, vol. 2, Constit. Emper.) Yet it cannot be permitted with a safe conscience that they freely blaspheme the Lord Jesus in their synagogues and curse Him, or that they seduce Christians, nor are marriages to be entered into with them unless the hope of conversion to the Christian faith shines forth, nor are negotiations or autonomy to be granted to them on Sundays and other Christian festivals, but rather they are to be treated as exiles and servants and marked with a certain sign of a harmful sect: Ἀναγκἀνῷ [sp.? “Compel”]. Liberty is to be permitted to those passing over to the Christians, and the way opened to them, with laws established for hearing evangelical sermons, and for attending instruction from the writings of the New Testament by those who are exceptionally skilled in the Hebrew language and the original text. Nor do those rescripts abolish such laws, provided that coercion of faith, which is hostile to conscience, is absent, since Lk. 14:23, ἀναγκασοὺς [compel] is prescribed for the ministry, not as civilly coercive, but morally persuasive. Let there be , however, a sincere intention of leading miserable men to the faith of Christ, and let those means by which we might win them over be piously employed, such as friendly admonitions and gentle persuasions (with harshness removed), and above all clear arguments and illustrious proofs from Scripture that conquer the mind: which God blesses, as the examples of many thousands converted to the Christian Faith from the 5th to the 15th century testify. See Jerome of the Holy Faith, Book Against the Jews, and the preface of the same; Beda, qv. 30, on 1 Kings; Council. Toletan. ch. 57 etc. Although indeed by the right of political superiority no one can be forced to the Faith, as Thomas teaches, pt. 2 of 2, q. 10, art. 8, yet that Jews cannot be compelled to hear the faith is Ἀναγκάζον [constraining], because this is purely extrinsic, and a παιδαγωγός [guide]: but that [faith] embraces an intrinsic act tending toward the intellect itself and the will.

Concerning the first, thus: it seems that they are not to be tolerated:

1. For they blaspheme both against Christ and against the blessed Virgin; they also persecute the catholic Faith, and they inflict injury upon the ecclesiastical sacraments, as is had in the Extravagants, On the Jews, Etsi Iudaeos. But blasphemers, according to the Old Law also, were to be handed over to death; therefore the Jews too are not to be tolerated, but to be exposed to death, especially those who conduct themselves thus.

2. Furthermore, in their book, which is called the Talmud, many things were contained that pertained to the blasphemy of Christ and the blessed Virgin; since therefore they observe the doctrine of that book as though it were a law, together with books of this sort they must be destroyed.

3. Likewise, Christians persecute pagans even to death, who are the holders of the Holy Land; but an insult to the Redeemer is a greater injury; therefore Christians ought to persecute those who perpetrate such an insult even to death; therefore they are not to be tolerated. But that they inflict an insult is evident from what is said in the Extravagants, On the Jews, In nonnullis. On the contrary: a. By what is said in the Psalm, on that verse: ‘Kill them not,’ the Gloss says: ‘This can be taken especially of the Jews;’ he prays that the Jews may not perish utterly: for they have indeed been dispersed in order that they may be provoked to conversion; and he also said concerning them: ‘Kill not those who killed me, but let the nation of the Jews remain with the sign of circumcision.’ They are to be tolerated. b. Likewise, testimony that is received from adversaries is stronger; but the catholic Church takes testimony from the Old Law, which the Jews observe; therefore, in order that the catholic Church may have testimony from enemies, the Jews are to be tolerated: for from the Old Law, namely from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, testimony about Christ is taken, which they cannot deny. c. Likewise, Isa. 10:22 has that the remnant of Israel shall be saved; and similarly the apostle says, Rom. 11:5; but the remnant could not be saved unless the seed of the Jews remained; therefore the seed of the Jews must be saved; therefore the Jews are to be tolerated. This must be granted. [Replies to objections:]

1. To the contrary objection, however, it must be said that although they commit blasphemy, still they believe that they are not sinning in this, because they do not yet believe that the Messiah has come, and in this they err and are reserved for future damnation unless they come to their senses, as is said on that verse of the Psalm: ‘I will repay them.’ The Gloss: ‘In the present however, they should persist in manifest blasphemy, so that they may be dispersed; in the future, so that they may be condemned. They ought to be restrained by secular princes, as is had in the Extravagants, On the Jews, In nonnullis, where it is said: in the provinces we most strictly forbid that they presume to burst forth into insult against the Creator; and since we ought not to conceal the reproach of Him who has wiped away our reproaches, we command that such presumptuous persons be restrained by secular princes with the addition of worthy punishment, lest they presume in any way to blaspheme the Crucified for us.

2. To the second it must be said that their books, in which blasphemies of this sort are contained, ought to be burned; but they themselves, if they should persist pertinaciously in blasphemy of this sort and are convicted before a judge, are to be punished with a fitting penalty. But it is otherwise if they blaspheme secretly.

3. To the third it must be said that there is a different reason concerning the pagan holders of the Holy Land themselves and concerning the Jews themselves. For Christians persecute those pagans as unjust holders and violators of a sacred place, to the injury of Christ; but the Jews are permitted to live and to dwell among Christians for many reasons, both because from the Jews we have received the Old Law, and because Christ came from that seed, then because the promise of their salvation was made; when the fullness of the gentiles shall have entered into Christ, they are to be restrained by due admonition; nor does it seem that greater pardon should be shown to them in manifest offenses than to evil Christians.

Second, it is asked whether their rites are as it were idolatry. That it seems so:

1. From the fact that it is said in Gal. 5:1, on the words, “Do not again be entangled with the yoke of bondage,” the Gloss says: “This bondage is not lighter than that of idolatry,” because the servitude of the legal observances is likened to idolatry in burden.

2. And again, it is said on the words in Gal. 4:9: “To whom do you wish to serve again?” the Gloss says: “The observance of the Law.” From this it is had that the servitude of the Law, to which they were then devoted, was a sin nearly equal to the servitude of idols, to which before their conversion they had been given over, and is as it were idolatry. And this is explained there by what follows: “The Law after Christ does not differ greatly from ancient idolatry”; it is manifestly shown that the servitude of the Law is now as it were idolatry. On the contrary. a. The Law prescribed believing in God and rendering to Him alone latria [worship]; but idolatry requires the contrary: for it rendered latria to the idols themselves; therefore the servitude of the Law is in no way equal to idolatry in sin. [Solution]: 1-2. To this it must be said that it is not an equal sin for the Jews themselves to observe the rite of the legal observances and to commit idolatry; but it is said to be a sin for those themselves who have assumed the Christian Faith, nearly equal because in both cases there is apostasy, though not equal. As to burden also it had likeness: for in both cases the burden was greatest, and therefore the sacrifices of the Jews were rejected just as those of the gentiles were. But it is said not to differ from idolatry because in both cases there was unbelief. For the Galatians, when they were gentiles, served the superstition of idolatry; but when they drew back from the catholic Faith, which forbade it, they again fell into the servitude of the legal observances, as it were into unbelief. Furthermore, by reason of the performed act, namely sacrifices, there was agreement with idolatry; also by reason of the propensity to sacrifice and of the superstition itself in sacrifices. Yet for the Jews it is not so great a sin now to adhere to the Law as was the sin of those who adhered to idols.

On occasion of this question it is asked whether those who come to the Faith from the Jews are to be received quickly or not, and similarly it can be asked concerning pagans. And it seems that not: a. from the fact that it is said in dist. 4, On Consecration, Jews, where it is said that for eight months they should enter within the catechumens of the church this threshold, and, if they are known to come with pure faith, only then should they merit the grace of baptism; the same is found there, Lest, which God forbid, where it is said that abstinence for forty days is enjoined. In both places therefore a great space of time is given for probation and for the work of penance to be carried out. But the contrary seems true:

1. From the fact that it is said, Acts 2:38, where Peter speaks to the Jews, saying: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.’ Since therefore they were baptized quickly, by his example it does not seem that reception into the Faith, or the sacrament of Faith, which is Baptism, should be deferred so long.

2. Likewise it is found, Acts 10:47-48, where it is said by Peter: ‘Can anyone forbid water, so that those who have received the Holy Spirit should not be baptized? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.’ Acts 8:36-38. From these things therefore it seems that so great a delay is not fitting. [Solution]: To which it must be said that things were otherwise in the primitive Church in part and otherwise in the progress of the Church. For in the primitive Church there was the gift of the Holy Spirit, which was also shown in a visible sign in believers; there were also other signs manifesting faith in them; on account of which it was not necessary to defer the sacrament of Faith. But in the progress of the Church, where there were no such signs showing or powerfully proving faith, and hypocrisy of heart was hidden or could be hidden, a delay of time was necessary, so that there might be a testing of faith and catechesis, through which there would be enabling for baptism. And therefore according to the different times a different term was appointed according to earlier and later, so that it might be clear concerning the enabling for faith and that the ease of returning to vomit might be removed in the judgment of a discerning prelate, according as more or less it shall seem expedient. But such a term is left to the judgment of a discerning prelate, according as more or less it shall seem expedient.

Secondly it is asked whether Jews or pagans can be over Christians or not. And it seems that yes:

1. From the fact that the apostle says, 1 Tim. 6:1: Let all who are under the yoke of slavery deem their masters worthy of all honor. Gloss: ‘Under the yoke of infidels.’ Therefore the apostle does not deny that infidels were able to be over the faithful.

2. Likewise, Extra, Of Many: Because to be cultivated. Therefore Jews can be over Christians. They have clung more longly to their lands, as owing to a contract of the place, let them remain for the cultivation of fields, rendering the customary payments to the aforesaid Christian men.

3. Likewise, they are able to receive a price for Christian slaves that have been purchased; which would not be the case unless they were able in some way to be over them, as is found in dist. 54, Fraternitatem.

4. It also seems so from what Gelasius says, XVII, question 4, where it is said that diligently. From this it seems that your care should faithfully examine the truth of affairs, so that neither religion may seem violated, nor a slave lying by this objection, strive to decline the rights of the rightful master, whom it is not certain to be a Christian, from the dominion of his master is not to be exempted. But the contrary seems true: a. From what is said in the Decretals, Multorum, where it is said: To no Jew. And it says that it is lawful to retain a Christian slave in his dominion, but, if any are found among them, let their freedom be preserved for them. Gregory: Whatever Christian slaves a Jew is found to have purchased, bring them without ambiguity to freedom according to the precepts of the laws, lest, God forbid, the Christian religion, made subject to the Jews, be polluted. b. Likewise, in dist. 54: No public offices are to be imposed on Jews by which they may be granted the punishment of inflicting upon Christians; let Christians have Jews as masters. But this was done so that to the Jews c. Likewise, it is found in the Decretals, On the Jews, where it is prohibited, To these things for all Christians. And this same thing is found there, when they expose themselves for some wage to the service of the Jews, as is continually said: Jews or Saracens, etc. But what reason is there that, on account of the Christian faith, the right over a slave should be taken away from him, since servitude was introduced by divine law and approved also by canon law? But the Christian religion does no wrong to anyone. [Solution]: To this it must be said that a Christian is not permitted to serve a Jew, on account of avoiding damage to the Christian religion, as is found in the Decretals, On the Jews, To these things for all, where it is said: The customs of the Jews and ours in no way agree. For this same reason also, if some, because of continual conversation and assiduous familiarity, are easily able to incline the minds of the simple to their superstition and faithlessness, and they themselves should be their slaves, let them be freed from their service, sometimes at a price being given, sometimes at no price being given. For a slave of a Jew is either homeborn or purchased. If homeborn, if he is or wishes to become a Christian, he is immediately snatched away into freedom, with no price given, as is found in the Code, On bishops, and dist. 54, Fraternitatem. But if he is purchased, either he was a Christian when he was bought or a pagan. If a Christian, he becomes free, with no price given; as is found in dist. 54, Mancipia, trade in Christians is forbidden to Jews, both by the law of the land and by the law of the forum. But if he was a pagan, either he was bought for the sake of service or for the sake of commerce. If for the sake of service, and he wishes to become a Christian, he becomes free without price, dist. 54, Fraternitatem. But in the second case, if within three months afterward he has not put him up for sale if he wishes to become a Christian, he is freed without price, because it is presumed that he bought him in order to serve. But if he has put him up for sale within that term and he wishes to become a Christian then or afterward, provided that the fault did not rest with the master so that he did not sell him, he is freed, the price of twelve solidi being returned by some Christian, dist. 54, Frater, and nitatem. Decretals, In the present council: If, however, a Jew shall circumcise one wishing to become a Christian, or shall imprint the mark of another sect, he is freed without price for the injury of his own body, dist. 54, Nulla, where it is said that if certain Christians have been defiled by them in Jewish rite or even circumcised, without the price being returned let them return to freedom and the Christian religion, but human law inflicts a heavier punishment. But what has been said about the slaves of the Jews can be said about the slaves of the Saracens: for the same suspicion and the same danger can exist in both. [To the objections]:

1. To the objection, however, on the contrary it must be said that that of the apostle is understood for the state of the primitive Church and so that unbelieving masters might be enticed to the conversion of faith through the services of faithful slaves. Hence the Gloss says: Rather, unbelieving masters are converted through the services of faithful slaves. But there is added there in the text: Lest the name of the Lord and doctrine be blasphemed. The Gloss: ‘As though of one invading what is another’s.’ According to that reasoning, it will seem to someone, and Christian doctrine will seem as if unjust, that it is also now so to be done. But to this it must be answered that another reason restores the pact. For now they ought not to serve, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed; for thus Jews and pagans are inclined to this, that they may draw the faithful into faithlessness or apostasy. On account of which cohabitation with Jews and pagans, unless for the sake of preaching, is forbidden, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. Nor ought Christian doctrine on this account to seem unjust, since the caution of faith must be preferred to all.

2. To the second, however, it must be said that, although Christians may cultivate the landed estates of Jews, they ought not nevertheless to serve Jews in their house, lest bad familiarity be contracted. And from this they are not said rightly to be over them as over slaves, because they cannot transfer them to another place or to another service, as is said in the Decretals, On the Jews. And this was done in favor of Christians, not of Jews, that they may cultivate the landed estates or lands bought from Jews, because they had formerly lived in those lands.

3. To the third, however, it must be said that, although they may receive the price of servitude, nevertheless not for Christians already existing, but for pagans who wish to become Christians. For by the law of the land Christian slaves are freed from the service of Jews, lest there be danger to the Christian faith. In favor also of the Christian faith, to certain men wishing to receive Christianity freedom is granted.

4. But that which is said in XVII, question 4, does not expressly give to understand that he was a Christian, but that he said that he had been a Christian from infancy, and that the mark of circumcision had been impressed on him by the aforesaid lord, he would be freed. But if he was not a Christian, he is not to be freed from servitude by the fact that he has fled to the church, unless he wishes to become a Christian, and this canon seems to say this. Hence it is not introduced for the dominion of Jews, but for the dominion of Christians: for some wished to defraud their master of his own right, fleeing to the enclosures of the Church.

5. To the last it must be said that the catholic Church intends to do injury to no one, but has ordered this so that no injury be done to God; but injury would be done to God if faith in something were endangered on account of the observance of temporal justice.

t:
Thirdly, it is asked whether the Jews are to be compelled to pay field tithes or the other things that Christians living in houses or dwelling in lands which are within the boundaries of some church are accustomed to pay. It seems that: a. For the Church must by no means be defrauded of its right; but it would be defrauded if Jews were to retain lands and not pay tithes; therefore they are to be compelled to payment. b. Furthermore, it was commanded in the Law of Moses that the sons of Israel should pay tithes to the Levites; similarly it is said in Mal. 3:10: Bring every tithe into my storehouse; and in 2 Chron. 31:5, where it is said that they were offering to God tithes of everything. Since, therefore, Jews are bound to the payment of tithes and are exempt from no privilege, since they are of worse condition and ought to be, by reason of sin, than they were in the time of the Law, they will now be bound to the payment of tithes. c. And if perhaps they should say that they would be bound to render them to their own Levites, against this it is that the Levitical priesthood yielded to the priesthood of Christ Himself, as is had in Heb. 7:12: The priesthood having been transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the Law also be made. Likewise in Daniel: When the Holy of holies has come. Therefore, Christ having come, your anointing ought to cease; the royal and priestly anointing ought to cease; therefore the payment of tithes was to be made to the priests of the New Law. d. Furthermore, tithes are rendered to God from lands in memory of the benefit of the annual multiplication of fruits; but lands are bounded according to the distinction of churches; therefore by reason of fields or lands tithes are to be paid by all who possess them; therefore Jews, if they possess lands, are bound to pay tithes to the churches. On the contrary:

1. Jews have nothing except from usury in most cases; but from usuries the Church ought to receive nothing; therefore, as it seems, neither ought it to receive anything from lands that have been bought with usuries.

2. Again, Sirach 34:21 says: The oblation of one sacrificing from injustice is defiled; and again: He who offers from the substance of the poor is as one who sacrifices a son in the sight of the father. The Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust. Since, therefore, these men have nothing except the gifts of the unjust, they ought not to be accepted by the Church, which receives in place of the Most High. [Solution]: To this it must be said that some tithes are predial and some are personal. Predial tithes, however, and whatever churches were wont to receive on account of fields, the churches can ask even from Jews by reason of the fields possessed by them, as is had in the Extra, De decimis, De terris, where it is said that Jews are to be compelled to pay tithes from the lands which they cultivate or to renounce the possessions altogether, lest perhaps the churches be able to be defrauded of their right on that account. Likewise it is had in the Extra, De usuris, Quanto, where it is said that Jews are to be compelled to make satisfaction to the churches for tithes and due oblations, which they are accustomed to receive from Christians from houses and other possessions, so that the churches may be preserved unharmed. Not that anything is to be received from usuries or from things acquired unlawfully, or that oblations are to be received in the church from the Jews themselves, but from things lawfully acquired by them by reason of the houses which they inhabit, lest the church be harmed excessively, if nevertheless the decency of the church in this matter is preserved. But if it should be contrary to decency and the church were not harmed excessively, one should refrain, to avoid scandal. [To the objections]:

1. And by this the contrary objection can be solved, because from usuries, insofar as they are such, the Church cannot ask tithes or oblations. And although lands may have been bought from usuries, nevertheless the Church can ask tithes, because the one who sold could sell only what he had by right, while the thing itself passes with its burden.

2. To the second, however, it must be said that, although oblations or gifts are not acceptable to God, insofar as they are offered by the unjust, nevertheless those things which are owed are acceptable, by reason of the fact that they are owed, if they are paid; whence in one respect they are acceptable, in another respect they are not acceptable; yet the action itself, which proceeds from a perverse will, is not acceptable. But when something is offered from theft or usury, it is not acceptable, because it is not offered from what is one’s own; but its restitution, insofar as it is such, would be acceptable.

t: Fourth, it is asked whether Christians can have a Jew or Saracen as a slave. It seems that they can: By what is said in XXIII, q. 8, Dispar, where it is said concerning Saracens, and in the Extra, De Iudaeis, where it is said that Jews were subjected by their own fault to perpetual servitude. Therefore Christians can have a pagan or Jew as a slave. This also obtains by custom in remote parts. On the contrary: 1. XXVIII, q. 1, where it is said: Whoever among those who have been baptized have not henceforth avoided the company of unbelievers, let them be given to Christians and let those men be publicly assigned to beatings. And there too: Let no cleric or layman dwell with Jews. And the apostle seems to give the reason, 1 Cor. 15:33: ‘Evil company corrupts good morals.’ [Solution]: To this it must be said that it is permitted for a Christian to have a pagan or Jew as a subject; yet he ought not to have familiarity with him, as is had in the Extra, De Iudaeis, Ad: for too great familiarity could be an occasion of drawing these men to the evil of unbelief. If, however, that man should wish to become a Christian in actuality, he ought not to be forbidden: for the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in such matters is not to be repelled. Nor by this is the service of the master taken away, but he ought to serve, or otherwise his liberation from servitude ought to be procured. To the objections: 1. However, it must be said in the contrary sense that from those authorities the subjection of servitude is not denied, but cohabitation of familiarity.

t: Whether a prince or magistrate may tolerate Jews in his city or province? Three things may be considered in the Jews. First, the sect and Jewish exercise. Second, usury. Third, hatred toward Christians. All these are evil and prohibited. The question is therefore whether a prince or magistrate may permit or tolerate these evils; and what may be a legitimate cause for permitting and tolerating them? I answer through the following conclusions: First Conclusion. A magistrate may permit the rites and exercises of the Jews if a sufficient cause is present. The Pope of Rome does this, as do many princes in their provinces. The cause may be threefold. First, that through Jewish rites the Christian truth may be shadowed forth and confirmed: St. Augustine, Of the City of God, bk. 18, ch. 46 and St. Thomas in pt. 2 of 2, quest. 10, art. 11, approve this cause. Second, that Jews who practice their rites and understand from the Christians among whom they dwell that those rites were merely shadows and figures of the Christian religion may more easily be converted to the Faith of Christ. St. Thomas, in the cited place, also approves this. Third, that Christian princes or magistrates, under the pretext of permission, may receive money and other gifts from the Jews to whom they permit the exercise. This is not lawful. For public sins, by which God is offended, cannot be permitted for the sake of temporal gain alone, which is hoped for from the permission. Second Conclusion. A magistrate may permit the usuries of the Jews if a sufficient cause is present. The Pope and other Christian princes also do this. The cause may be twofold. One, to prevent a greater evil. For if, as I said above, usuries were not permitted, many thefts, robberies, oppressions of the poor and similar inconveniences would occur. Therefore, to avoid these evils, usuries may be permitted as a lesser evil. The other, that Christian princes and magistrates who permit the usuries of the Jews may be participants in the profit. This is not lawful. For it is certain that usury is prohibited by natural and divine law; and the profit that is acquired through usury is mere theft. Just as, therefore, the Jews sin against justice by receiving usurious profit, so do the Christians who are participants in that profit. They are considered to be participants, however, when they permit usuries for the purpose of being able to receive profit therefrom. This conclusion must be limited in two ways: First, that common usuries may be permitted which do not exceed the profit permitted by law and custom, but not exorbitant usuries, of which I shall speak shortly. Second, that a Christian magistrate may not receive profit from usuries on account of the mere permission of usuries: although they may receive it under another title. And indeed under a double title: First, the title of punishment; because he may punish the Jews on account of usuries; and the profit that has been unjustly acquired from usuries he may either restore to its owners or convert to public utility. Then, the title of exaction; because he may exact an annual tribute or tax from the Jews, not by reason of the permission of usuries, but by reason of the granted habitation in a Christian place. Third Conclusion. A Christian magistrate or prince cannot with a good conscience permit or leave unpunished the hatred of Jews toward Christians. Note: Hatred is twofold: The one is internal; because since it is hidden, the magistrate cannot punish it. The other is external, which breaks out into open injury. This ought to be coerced by the magistrate. We say, therefore, that such hatred, when it is exercised by Jews against Christians, can in no way be permitted or tolerated, but must be severely punished: and the prince sins gravely if he does not punish those who commit offenses. The reason is that a prince is bound by his office to punish every public injury, if he is able, so that justice may be preserved: therefore, he is also bound to punish the injury which the Jews commit against Christians. This is, indeed, manifold: First, because they exact immoderate and intolerable usury from citizens, country folk, and the poor. Whatever they exact beyond the principal is theft. Therefore, they commit intolerable theft. Second, by exacting such usury, they harm the republic or the community greatly. For a republic cannot stand or flourish when the people are oppressed and exhausted by usury. Third, besides usury, another injury is added. For whatever is for sale in the market, the Jews snatch away from the Christians by offering a higher price to the sellers than other buyers are accustomed to offer; and afterwards, which is most iniquitous, Christians are forced to pay double the price to the Jews if they wish to buy what is necessary for feeding their families. Fourth, so that they may do all these things with impunity, they distribute gifts to the officials of princes so that they may be protected by them. Fifth, from this it happens that the people, who bear such injuries with difficulty, become prone to inciting sedition, both against the Jews themselves and against their defenders and patrons. Against the Jews, indeed, because they are thieves and plunderers; against the patrons, because they are partners of thieves and plunderers. If a prince or magistrate does not prevent or punish these great evils (to say nothing of the rest), he is a participant in the crime and is bound to restitution. He can, however, prevent them in three ways. First, if he expels the Jews entirely from his province or city. Second, if he does not indeed expel them, but forces them to agriculture, or to mechanical arts, or to exercise other works; and does not allow them to live in idleness and luxury, as they now live. Third, if he deprives them of all the money and wealth which they have received through usury. Would that these things were brought into practice. You will say, if the Jews are either expelled or do not accept usury, two inconveniences will follow: First, because Christian princes in time of necessity will not have money for war. For they are accustomed to seek this from the Jews. Then, the subjects of the princes, who are in need of money, will not be able to borrow. I respond: The contrary follows: First, because once the Jews are expelled, the citizens will be able to contribute more support than the Jews are accustomed to. For whatever the Jews contribute, they receive from the citizens through unjust usury. And not only this, but also whatever is necessary for them to sustain their lives. Therefore, they take two portions from the citizens: one, which they give to the prince; the other, by which they live. Certainly, if the Jews were expelled, the citizens would be prepared to give either both portions to their prince, or at least no less than they give to the Jews. Next, the subjects of princes are in greater need of money when the Jews are present than when they are absent. For when they are present and demanding intolerable usury, they are completely drained. If they were absent, or at least did not demand such immoderate usury, the subjects would be less drained, and consequently would be in less need of money. Our Adam Contzen has written extensively on this subject in his Politics.

t: Despite its many weaknesses, this earlier work remains a landmark of scholarship in the field… At that time, the only serious attempt to document this development was Ritschl’s Die christliche Lehre von der Rechtfertigung und Versohnung (1870). The value of that work was rather reduced by the moralist assumptions Ritschl brought to his task, and by his decision to limit his analysis from the eleventh to the nineteenth century, focusing particularly on German-language Protestant contributions to the discussion. The vast scholarly undertakings which have given the modern period the magnificent critical editions denied to Ritschl (such as the Weimar Luther edition) have also cast new light on the theology of the medieval period, calling into question many of Ritschl’s conclusions. One of the more troubling aspects of my investigation was the realisation that most of Ritschl’s conclusions, particularly his very unsatisfactory account of Luther’s theological formation, could no longer be sustained.” – McGrath, Iustitia Dei, 3rd ed., Preface, vii, ix-x McGrath, Alister – Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification 3rd ed. rev. In the text [of Rom. 3:23-26] we have the eight following things:

1. The persons justified – (i) Sinners; (ii) Such sinners of all sorts that shall believe, whether Jews or Gentiles.

2. The justifier, or efficient cause – God.

3. The impulsive cause – grace.

4. The means effecting, or material cause – the redemption of Christ.

5. The formal cause – the remission of sins.

6. The instrumental cause – faith.

t: There are innumerable passages in Scripture in which forgiveness of sins is attributed to good works, proceeding from faith and the special aid of grace. to mot for the present that passage, St. James 2:24, where man is expressly said to be ‘justified by works, and not by faith only;’ to omit, I say, that passage, about the meaning of which there is such warm contention between the parties, and of which we will afterwards treat in its proper place, see Eze. 17:21, and 33:12, 14-16, 19; Mt. 6:14; 18:35; Lk. 6:37; James 5:19-20, etc. Nay, any one who attentively reads the Scriptures will find that there are perhaps more passages which exact the condition of good works for obtaining the pardon of sins and eternal life, than there are which require the condition of faith, simply so called (Apology for the Remonstrants’ Confession, ch. 22, p. 237 verso); although it [i.e. faith] is necessarily always understood (nay rather presupposed) in them all. Let whoever chooses consult the Collection of passages for good works taken from both Testaments by G. Wicelius (Coacervatio locorum utriusque Testamenti de absoluta necessitate bonorum operum), and others; but especially let him diligently, and without prejudice, read the Holy Scriptures themselves. Scripture also very frequently teaches that we are purged from sins by the participation of the sacraments. (Eph. 5:26; Acts 2:38; 22:16; Tit. 3:5-7; Mt. 26:27-28 and frequently others)

t: 18th Objection [by Osiander]: Christ has brought us eternal justice. This applied justice is not eternal: Therefore this is not our justice, but God Himself is our justice. Answer: The Lord is our justice, that is, our Justifier. But that our applied justice is eternal, has been showed before; because the imputation thereof is continued to all eternity. That justice also of the Law which is begun in us in this life, shall be continued, and perfected in the life to come. But that justice which is God Himself is not in us: because so God should be an accident to his creature, and become justice in man. For justice and virtue are things created in us, not the essence of God. Moreover Osiander, who obiects this, does not discern the cause from the effect. As we live not, or are wise by the essence of God (for this is all one, as to say, that we are as wise as God) so also we are not just by the essence of God. Wherefore nothing is more impious than to say that the essential justice of the Creator is the justice of the creatures: for thereof it would follow, that we have the justice of God, yea the very essence of God. The cause must be discerned from the effect, increate iustice from created justice.

t: Objection: Faith is never without good works. Therefore, it cannot justify alone. Response. Faith may be said to justify without good works in two ways: either in such a way that we say the faith which justifies does not have good works joined with it, or in such a way that we say good works are not co-causes of justification. Faith indeed is never without good works; yet it does not follow from this that good works are a co-operating cause concurring with faith unto justification. Thus, the sun never gives light without heat, yet heat is not a co-operating cause which concurs with the sun unto illumination. So faith does not justify as separated from good works, nor yet for that reason are good works a co-operating cause of our justification.

t: Obedience to all God’s commandments is covenanted (Dt. 7:1• & 10, 12; Jer. 7:23; Lev. 19:17-18; Lk. 10:27; Mk. 12:30), not as the cause of life, but as the qualification and effect of faith, and as the way to life. Faith that embraces life is obedient and fruitful in all good works; but in one sort faith is the cause of obedience and good works, and in another of justification and eternal life. These it seeks in the promises of the covenant; those it works and produces, as the cause does the effect. Faith was the efficient cause of that precious oblation in Abel (Heb. 11:4, 7, etc.), of reverence and preparing the ark in Noah, of obedience in Abraham; but it was the instrument only of their justification. For it does not justify as it produces good works, but as it receives Christ, though it cannot receive Christ unless it brings forth good works. A disposition to good works is necessary to justification, being the qualification of an active and lively faith. Good works of all sorts are necessary to our continuance in the state of justification, and so to our final absolution, if God give opportunity; but they are not the cause of, but only a preceding qualification or condition to final forgiveness and eternal bliss. If then, when we speak of the conditions of the covenant of grace, by “condition” we understand whatsoever is required on our part, as precedent, concomitant, or subsequent to justification, repentance, faith, and obedience are all conditions; but if by “condition” we understand what is required on our part as the cause of the good promised, though only instrumental, faith or belief in the promises of free mercy is the only condition. Faith and works are opposed in the matter of justification and salvation in the covenant, not that they cannot stand together in the same subject—for they are inseparably united—but because they cannot concur or meet together in one and the same court to the justification or absolution of man. For in the court of justice, according to the first covenant, either being just he is acquitted, or unjust he is condemned; but in the court of mercy, if you receive the promise of pardon, which is done by a lively faith, you are acquitted and set free, and accepted as just and righteous; but if you do not believe, you are sent over to the court of justice. Obedience is twofold: [1] Perfect in measure and degree—this is so far required that, if it be not performed, we must acknowledge our sin in coming short. And this God is pleased to exact at our hands, that we might walk in humility before him, strive after perfection, and freely acknowledge his rich grace and mercy in accepting and rewarding the best service we can render to his Highness, when in the court of justice it deserves to be rejected. [2] Sincere, uniform, and constant, though imperfect in measure and degree; and this is so necessary that without it there is no salvation to be expected. The covenant of grace calls for perfection, yet accepts sincerity, God in mercy pardoning the imperfections of our best performances. If perfection were rigidly exacted, no flesh could be saved; if it were not at all commanded, imperfection would not be sin, nor would perfection be something to be labored after. The faith that is lively to embrace mercy is ever joined with an unfeigned purpose to walk in all well-pleasing, and the sincere performance of all holy obedience, as opportunity is offered, ever attends that faith by which we continually lay hold upon the promises once embraced. Actual good works of all sorts (though not perfect in degree) are necessary to the continuance of actual justification, because faith can no longer lay faithful claim to the promises of life than it does virtually or actually lead us forward in the way to heaven. For if we say we have fellowship with God and walk in darkness, we lie and do not the truth; but if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another (1 John 1:6–7). This walking in the light, as He is in the light, is that qualification whereby we become immediately capable of Christ’s righteousness, or actual participants of his propitiation, which is the sole immediate cause of our justification, taken for remission of sins or actual approbation with God. The truth of this doctrine St. John likewise ratifies in terms equivalent in the words immediately following: “And the blood of Christ cleanses us (walking in the light as God is in the light) from all sin.” (1 Jn. 1:7) But of these things more fully in their several degrees, as this covenant has been revealed. In this covenant man promises to repent of his sins, and, repenting, to cleave to the promise of mercy made in Jesus Christ, and in faith to yield willing, cheerful, and continual obedience. In contracts among men, one may ask more and another bid less, and yet they may come to agreement; but it is altogether fruitless for men to think of entering into covenant with God if they are not resolved to obey in all things. The practice of all God’s people who have ever made covenant with Him expressly declares as much when they solemnly entered into or renewed their covenant. For thus they promise: “Whatever the Lord says, that we will do” (Exod. 24:3, 7). The people said to Joshua, “The Lord our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey” (Josh. 24:23). And they entered into a covenant to seek the Lord God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul, so that whoever would not seek the Lord God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman (2 Chron. 15:12–13). And the king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book; and all the people stood to the covenant (2 Chron. 34:31; 2 Kings 23:3). They entered into a curse and into an oath to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our God, and his judgments and his statutes (Neh. 10:29). And thus runs the exhortation of Joshua to the two tribes and a half when he sent them home: “Take diligent heed to do the commandments of the law, which Moses the servant of the Lord charged you, to love the Lord your God, and to walk in all his ways, and to keep his commandments, and to cleave to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Josh. 22:5). This must not be understood as if one who, through frailty and infirmity, offends in any one jot or tittle should be counted a covenant-breaker; for then no man would be innocent. Rather, the promise must be interpreted according to the rule of obedience given, which calls for perfection but accepts sincerity. In the covenant of mercy we bind ourselves to believe and rest upon God with the whole heart, so that doubting or distrust arising from weakness and infirmity must indeed be acknowledged as sin, yet every such frailty does not prove the person to be a transgressor of the covenant. The same holds true of obedience. But of this more fully when treating the particular manner in which God has been pleased to administer this covenant.

III.21: so the internal instrumental cause is not hope, charity, fear, repentance, etc., but faith alone among causes of its own order — and alone indeed not by reason of its existence, but by reason of its apprehension and the faculty of apprehending — inasmuch as it alone is the analogous instrument suited to the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ.

Faith, moreover, is considered in the act of justification neither dispositively, nor habitually, nor formally, nor meritoriously, nor in the genus of a work, but partly organically by reason of its own act, and partly correlatively by reason of its object [i.e. Christ]. Whence the apostle wisely says that we are justified πίστει [pistei, by faith], ἐκ πίστεως [ek pisteōs, out of faith], διὰ τῆς πίστεως [dia tēs pisteōs, through faith] — but never διὰ τὴν πίστιν [dia tēn pistin, on account of faith].

t: When we say, ‘Faith alone does justify,’ we do not mean fidem solitariam, that faith which is alone; neither do we in construction join sola with fides the subject, but with justification the predicate, meaning that true faith though it be not alone, yet it does justify alone, even as the eye, though in respect of being it is not alone, yet in respect of seeing, unto which no other member does concur with it, it being the only instrument of that faculty, it is truly said to see alone, so faith though in respect of the being thereof it is not alone, yet in respect of justifying, unto which act no other grace does concur with it, it being the only instrument of apprehending and receiving Christ, is truly said to justify alone. When we say by faith only, this opposes all other graces of the same order, but not the merits of Christ or the efficacy of God’s grace; the apostle, Rom. 4, makes it all one to prove a man justified by grace, Christ and by faith. It is to be considered as alone in the act of justification, but not in the subject justified; therefore that is a reproach cast on Protestants to call them Solifidians.

t: But now comes a greater question: If by justification our sins be forgiven us, what sins are forgiven I pray? sins past, or sins to come? We are taught that in the instant of justification all our sins past and to come are remitted; which is in my mind an unsound doctrine: for if we look narrowly into it, we shall find that in propriety of speech, remission of sins has relation to that which is past; it’s said therefore, Rom. 3:25: ‘Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past through the forbearance of God.’ And remission of sins has relation to those that are past, as appears by inevitable reason; for what is remission of sins, but sin covered? Now can a thing be covered before it be? ‘Blot out mine iniquities,’ etc. says David; can a thing be blotted out before it’s written? This is the thing [that] makes the Pope so ridiculous, that he will forgive sins for the time before they are committed; but what, do we get nothing for the time to come? Yes, yes, when the sin is past, by faith we have a new access unto God; and having risen by repentance, we get a new act, not of universal justification, but of a particular justification, from this and that particular sin. But if there be forgiveness of sins past already, and I know that I am justified, and my sins remitted: may I now pray for forgiveness of sins past? The Papists say it is active infidelity, and as absurd as to pray to God to create the world anew, or incarnate his Son again. But there is no conversion where there is no praying; and there is need of praying for the remission of sins past, and against sin for the time to come, as I shall show next time; as also consider whether there be any interruption of the act of justification by falling into great sins. There’s no man has a mind more against quirks and quillets than I; yet for the opening of these things, and staying and settling the mind, and clearing the understanding, give me leave the next time to clear these things unto you.

t: It has been commonly said by some of our best divines that justification is transacted in our first union and incorporation into Christ; at which time it is conceived that the pardon of all sin is sealed to the believer at once. But I fear the misunderstanding of this point (not untrue in itself, if not mistaken and misapprehended) has laid the ground upon which some build that unhappy structure which turns the grace of God into wantonness: who knows not that justification in the proper acceptation of the word, according to the Scripture phrase, is the act of a judge pronouncing a judicial sentence, wherein he absolves the person of the sinner from all sin and punishment due to him for sin, and that for the alone righteousness of the surety Christ freely imputed, and by faith received of him. And according to this, I suppose we shall not err from the truth, if we say: 1. That the main work of justification, is even as yet to us future, viz. at the great and last day of Judgment, when we shall receive a final quietus est, and discharge, and when God shall wipe away all tears from our eyes: And yet 2. That in our first union with Christ there is a work of justification, viz. actual imputation of Christ’s righteousness, and actual remission of what sin for the present the soul stands guilty of, at that time when it is first united to Christ. I dare not say that justification, quatenus [so far as] it comprehends imputation and remission of sin, is one individual act; or that all sins, past, present and to come are remitted to the believer at once; but this I say, that in our first union, all our sins past and present are actually pardoned; and this favor received is a pledge of assurance that in future also, by applying ourselves to Christ, we may and shall receive the forgiveness of our daily sins, and that at the Last Day we shall at once be absolved from all accusations and charges laid in against us; and that justification (besides those particular acts of pardon, and imputation of Christ’s righteousness) does connote a state that the subject at his first believing is put into, viz. a state of grace, and favor, and reconciliation with God for the imputed righteousness of Christ, without apostasy from it, either total or final.
