t:
This question is not proposed without cause by us: for on the one hand, if God’s simplicity and immutability are regarded, it will not seem in any way admissible in God that wills be contrary to one another; which also will always be done according to that saying: ‘My will shall be done: and whatsoever He hath willed He hath done.’ Yet if many passages which are handed down in Scripture be considered, we should confess: there is no one who would not say that the will of God is not one only but in a manner manifold: and very often contrary. For He commands many things which do not happen either because He cannot effect them to be, or because He does not will them to be. The former cannot be said without denying God’s omnipotence, and thus deity. Some distinguish between an antecedent will and a consequent will: as [John] Damascus, bk. 2, ch. 46. Others between the will of good-pleasure and the will of sign: as Lombard and the scholastics: Sentences, bk. 1, dist. 45. Others between a will not revealed and a will revealed. Others between absolute volition and conditional volition. Others what God wills to be done respecting us, and into the will which He wills to be from us. Some distinguish in the will of the Almighty a will efficacious and an inefficacious will, as Augustine in the Enchiridion, chs. 102-3. These divisions seem various, but if they be weighed diligently and rightly understood, they reduce to the same. … Efficacious & Inefficacious Will Thirdly, that former and absolute will is also called by Augustine, just as it is most certain, so also most omnipotent, efficacious and invincible: and this is because it is always fulfilled, as much in heaven as on earth. But the other, namely the conditional, is called by the same Augustine the inefficacious will: because, clearly, it is not always fulfilled. For since it depends on conditions which God demands of us, and we do not perform them, it happens that it is not always nor in all things fulfilled, and therefore it is deservedly called inefficacious, namely by itself alone. Let Augustine be read in volume 3, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chs. 102-3. Some things also in volume 5, On the City of God, bk. 22, chs. 1-2. …

IV. From those things which I have said, it appears, first, why, although there is only one will of God—that is, one decree concerning all things, as has been demonstrated, and that immutable—it is nevertheless said to be manifold: namely, both on account of the diverse kinds of things which God wills, and on account of the diverse manner of willing, as it seems to us: because, namely, he wills some things simply and absolutely, while other things seem to us to be willed conditionally. Then it is also clear that, although there seem to be many partitions of the divine will, all are nevertheless reduced to one partition: namely, to the absolute and secret will, which is also called the will of Good Pleasure; and to the revealed and conditional will, which is not undeservedly named the will of the sign. And thus, in the third place, it appears that, although in reality there is only one will in God, as has been declared and confirmed, it can nevertheless be said to be manifold by different respects. And conversely, although on account of the diverse reasons by which he seems to will, and by which he explains his will, many wills of his are said to exist: it does not therefore hinder that there is in reality only one will of God, and that constant and eternal: which is the head of this our thesis. For although He wills many things, and indeed willed some things, for example, in the Old Testament, but wills other things in the New: yet He willed both those and these by the same will and decree. He willed those at one time, namely, until the time of correction, as the Apostle says: he wills these at another time, until the end of the world. Behold how the diverse kinds of things which he wills do not in the least cause there to be in reality many wills of God: but one and the same will always remains in God. And although he seems to will many things absolutely, but others conditionally: in reality, however, if one must speak properly, all things whatsoever God wills, He wills absolutely and simply. And consequently, all things which He wills also come to pass. For the fact that he is said to will certain things conditionally: this is to be referred only to the manifestation of that will. For there is no conditional will in God, because this fights against his eternal wisdom: but only in the law. And this also, that He signifies in the law that He wills conditionally: He had decreed by his absolute will to do—namely, not to manifest his will concerning the saving or damning of men without a condition; and this because this would be both useful to us and would conduce to the manifesting of his justice. For it was and is useful to us the elect to know that God does not will that anyone be saved without living faith in Christ: and consequently, if we wish to be saved, that we must believe in Christ. Likewise, this conduced to rendering the reprobate inexcusable. For they know what things are necessary for salvation: and consequently, it served to vindicate the justice of God from all accusations and calumnies. Therefore, because it was expedient, He revealed his will with a condition. And in this respect, the will of God seems to be twofold: which, however, is in reality only one, and that firm and constant. For by one and constant will he absolutely wills only the elect to be saved: and consequently He wills only also by true faith, which can be kept, are given: but the reprobate, are absolutely excluded from this salvation: and therefore, are not given the faith by which they can be blessed in heaven. See how the different modes, by which God seems to will, do not remove the fact that there remains but one, eternal and absolute and immutable will of God, on account of which different modes, different wills also seem to exist.

V. But that He also commands many things to be done, which are not done: it does not follow from this, however, either that He is impotent: as if He could not cause that what He commands, be done: or that there is truly a manifold will in God: one, which He signifies by word, another, which He does not will to be done in His presence, that which He commands. For there are two kinds of God’s commandments: some are simply absolute: and without any condition at all, either expressed or tacit. These are the most certain, absolute and simple testimonies of the divine will, which is called good pleasure. Such was that to Moses, do all things according to the pattern which you saw on the mountain. Likewise, Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: go into Egypt: and other commands of that kind made both to Moses himself and to the prophets. Because these are the very will of God: therefore He who gives these commands, also brings it about that they are done. And of these is that in Isaiah 46, ‘My counsel shall stand: and my will shall be done;’ and Pm. 115, ‘Whatsoever He willed, He did.’ Therefore, as far as this kind of God’s commandments is concerned: it appears that there is one and the same will: that, namely, which is revealed in the Word: and that, which was hidden in the secret counsel of God. Whence does this appear? From the fact that what God commands happens. There are other commandments, which He promulgated with a condition, if not expressed, at least tacit: such as those which we have in the law. Namely, if we wish to enter into life: that this and that is commanded to us, and that these commandments are to be kept, as Christ explained, saying: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. All these things indeed, are proposed conditionally both to the elect and to the reprobate: meanwhile, however, these commandments have a far different reason, insofar as they are made to the elect: and another, insofar as they are made to the reprobate. Insofar as they are made to the elect: although they are proposed with a condition: yet the will of God in them is absolute. For God simply wills: that they be kept by the elect, if not always, at least at length sometime. And for this reason, because they cannot perform these things by their own strength: He gives them the strength of the Spirit, by which they can; just as He promises through Ezekiel: I will cause that you walk in my commandments. And because even with the strength which the Lord supplies, they cannot perfectly keep the commandments in themselves: He brings it about that they keep them perfectly in Christ: insofar as namely: And through Christ their transgressions are not imputed to them: and on account of Christ, their begun obedience, serving as most perfect, is accepted: and on the contrary, Christ’s justice and obedience are imputed to them: and because finally, at the end in heaven most perfectly, even in themselves, they will complete the sum of the law. In this way also it appears, that the will of God, which is revealed in the commandments: is one and the same in reality with the secret will and will of good pleasure. Therefore, neither here are there two different wills, but one. God acts in giving the law to the elect, as a parent in prescribing laws to his children. He not only teaches what He requires of them: but also signifies that He altogether wills that they keep them, whether they want to or not. But towards the reprobate, He acts as a Lord towards his servants. He will promulgate merely conditional laws: if they want to be with Him, [He wills] altogether that they conduct themselves thus: if not, let them depart. Thus God. Therefore, insofar as these commandments are given to the reprobate, and likewise promises are added to them: all are truly conditional. For the will of God is not absolute, that the reprobate keep them: or attain the promises. This is clear, both from the one example of ‘Pharaoh, I will harden, lest he let the people go:’ and from the fact that they do not keep them, neither in themselves, nor in Christ: in whom they are not: nor ever will keep them. But those things which God properly wills: He brings it about that all of them be accomplished: according to that, All things, whatsoever He willed, He did: And that in Isa. 46, ‘My counsel shall stand, and my will shall be done.’ Wherefore there is not here a double will of God in reality: one in the law, another in the mind and essence of God: for it is not the will of God that the impious should keep the law, as has been said. No one, therefore, will be able to infer in any way from the precepts of God that there is a double will in reality. I will speak more briefly and clearly. The Law can be considered in two ways: either insofar as it is Torah (doctrine), by which it is taught what is pleasing to God, and what must be done by us, or not done, if we wish to be saved: in this way the Law is taught as pertaining to all, both the reprobate and the elect. And because it reveals and teaches what is right and pleasing to God: that is therefore said to be the will of God, because it reflects the nature of God, and what God loves and approves. Or it is considered insofar as it is Torah (commandment): that is, the true testimony of the secret will, or what He wills to be done by us at all. In this way it pertains only to the elect. This will of God, revealed in the law, is fulfilled by the elect: in the way that was mentioned above: and as God wills it to be done by them. The impious, however, the reprobate, while they act against the doctrine of the law, and thereby against their own duty: they do not act against the absolute, true, and properly so-called will of God: but they are said to act against the will of God for this reason, because they act against that which they know to be pleasing to God, and to be approved by God. But if you object that they therefore do not properly sin, because they do not act against the will of God, which is properly the will of God: that exception is easily refuted. For sin is defined, not as what is a transgression of the secret will and divine good pleasure: but as what is a transgression of the divine law: and what is 1 Jn. 3:4, lawlessness (anomia). For we sin for this reason, because we do not perform the things that are good and pleasing to God, and commanded and owed by us, but the contrary. In the law, however, are manifested: what all men owe to God by duty, and what they do not owe. Therefore, they sin more gravely who act against these things, and are therefore said to sin against the will of God: because they sin against that doctrine by which we are taught what is consistent with the nature of God, and what we owe Him by duty: and what is in itself pleasing and acceptable to God. But if you object again: but God therefore mocks the reprobate: when He commands that they do this or that: if this is not His certain and definite will. He does not mock them at all: because by His law, although He does not reveal what He absolutely wills to be done by them (for this is properly the will of God), yet He clearly teaches what is the duty of Him and of every man. Therefore, the law is deservedly called by Moses, Torah (doctrine): because it teaches everyone what his duty is: adding moreover, that whoever has acted against this duty of his, sins gravely and becomes liable to death. On the contrary, he who has done his duty: him [He rewards]. Lest this seem insufficient to you? Or is this mocking? Tell me, I pray: In the parable of the Gospel, those who were first invited to the wedding, and did not come: was it therefore a mockery to them by the king: because he only signified to them what would be pleasing to him, and what was their duty: and did not command them to be compelled, as the second ones, to come to the wedding? Not at all. Yet meanwhile, the will of the king in inviting the first was not that which it was in the second. For in calling these latter, the will of the king was absolute: that they should come at all, and therefore he also brought it about that they should come at all. To the former, however, he only signified: and that candidly and ingenuously: what would be pleasing to Him. As therefore it cannot be said that He called the first to the wedding with an invitation: although the will of the King was not absolute and simple that they come, as it was in calling the second: so neither can it be said that God mocks the reprobate when He gives them the law and calls them: although it is not His will that they come and obey the law. For it is enough to render them inexcusable: that they understand what things are pleasing to God, and what is their duty what things are pleasing to God, and what is their duty: they would have taken and thought that they were doing it by their own virtue, from God, who has absolute right over them and over all, to be commanded. To that point, that God commanded Abraham to kill his son, when nevertheless He did not want him killed: and to Pharaoh, to let the people go, when nevertheless He did not want them to be let go: and from this many try to gather that there were two, and those contrary, wills in God: one expressed by word, the other hidden in His own mind: We answer that this does not follow at all. For there was only one, and that a constant will: namely, that Abraham’s son was not to be killed: nor was the people to be let go by Pharaoh: and thus both were fulfilled. But as for the command given to Pharaoh, it was a doctrine by which He signified what was to be done by Pharaoh if he did not want to be afflicted by so many plagues: and what was his duty, and in itself just and owed: but it was not a testimony of His absolute will. Wherefore it does not follow from that that there were two wills of God. In the command also given to Abraham, it was not a simple will of God that he should kill his son: but only that he should take the sword, with the intention of killing and sacrificing, and that for the sake of God: and thus show his piety towards God, and his promptness in obeying: which was also entirely done: because this was the will of God. But the will of God did not extend as far as the killing. Therefore, when Abraham, having finished all other things, had extended the sword with which he might slaughter his son: the Lord forbade him to do it. To which will also Abraham complied. Thus neither here was there a double will of God: but one. And the Lord said: offer your son as a burnt offering: this therefore was the will of God: and yet afterwards, He signified another will. It was not another: for He did not first want that it should come to the actual slaughter. Therefore Moses premises, The Lord tempted Abraham: but He only wanted that, with other things actually performed, he should also slaughter him with the promptness of his mind, not with the sword. For this is that which, first and properly, the Lord requires in His precepts: that is, that we should be prompt in mind for His obedience, and by this promptness of our mind of ours, the commandments are properly fulfilled before God. The sum in almost all these arguments is admitted as a parable: for the will of God, properly accepted, is the absolute, certain, and firm decree of God, concerning things to be done, either by Himself or by others: and that this is always fulfilled, and is immutable, we do not doubt to affirm. But the Law and all commandments are called the will of God: because by them it is signified and taught what is in itself just, and pleasing to God: and what is required of us, if we wish to be saved. But alone, it is not properly the will of God: but the Torah, the doctrine of the just: and the command of doing it. But if with this doctrine and command there is joined the decree of God, by which He absolutely wills that what He requires be performed: then it will be said to be properly the will of God: as it is, in so far as it is given to the elect. Wherefore not undeservedly they have distinguished in the schools, not indeed the will of God itself: but the signification of the name of the will of God: in so far as it sometimes signifies the decree of God itself, and the good-pleasure: which is properly called will: whence it is also called the will of good-pleasure, and absolute will, because it is without condition: and most omnipotent, because it is always done. But sometimes it signifies that which is in itself pleasing to God, and just: and which the nature of the divine genius refers to: and which is required of us, if we wish to be saved: which is properly called law, and Torah: whence also will is signified: because by this doctrine it is signified what is pleasing to God, and what is of our duty: And conditional will, because these things are required of us, if we wish to obtain eternal salvation. In truth, however, the will of God, properly accepted, is only one, and that perpetual, and firm: as has now been sufficiently and abundantly declared.

t: But against this it may be objected what St. Peter [and Timothy] says: that He would have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his will. (2 Pet. 3 [v. 9]; 1 Tim. 2:4) And therefore either there are diverse and contrary wills in God, or it is his will that all should be saved, but yet are not, because they will not believe. I answer: That the will of God is diversely distinguished by the doctors, as [John] Damascene (The will of God is not diverse, Damascene, bk. 2, ch. 46), into an: 1. Antecedent will 2. Consequent will Lombard and the Schoolmen (bk. 1, ch. 45) into his: 1. Signified will 2. Well-pleasing will Tertullian (Lib. Exhort. ad castitatem.), into his: 1. Efficient will 2. Permissive will Whereof he calls the first voluntas pura and the other voluntas indulgentiae. St. Augustine (Enchiridion, ch. 102 & 103), into his: 1. Effectual working and omnipotent will 2. Not working, or not efficient will Others into his: Absolute will Conditional will Others into his Secret will Revealed will All which, and all such like distinctions of God’s will, if they be diligently observed and well understood, do fall into the same end and do no ways prove either diverse wills to be in God or any contradiction to be in the will of God. For it is most certain that as the essence of God is most simple, without composition or division, so the will of God, which is nothing else but his eternal decree concerning all things, is one and the selfsame immutable and unresistible: in so much that the wicked, who as much as in them lies, do resist the will of God revealed and commanded unto us in his Word, yet notwithstanding, will they, nill they, they fulfill the will of God decreed in Himself from all eternity; as you may see most plainly in the example of Pilate, Herod and the wicked Jews, who in crucifying Christ, rebelled and resisted the will of God revealed in his word, yet herein they did perform the secret will of God, which before all worlds He had determined should be done, as St. Peter shows (Acts 2:23; Augustine in Enchiridion, ch. 98), Et sic in hoc ipso quod contra voluntatem Dei fecerunt, de ipsis facta est voluntas eius: And so in this very thing wherein they did against God’s will, God effected his own will. (Idem, de cor. et gratia) Et de his qui faciunt quod non vult, facit ipse, quae vult: And touching these men which do against his will, He does whatsoever He will.

t: Again, revelation is either uncreated or created. There is an uncreated revelation which is infinite, and such is that which the Father reveals to the Son from all eternity. The created revelation hath three degrees, 1. Imperfect, 2. Perfect, 3. And most perfect. The most perfect revelation is in Christ-man, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The perfect revelation is in angels and blessed souls in heaven: the imperfect is in men on earth. The revelation vouchsafed to men on earth is either ineffectual or effectual. The ineffectual is a revelation not available to salvation, such is that revelation which may befall wicked men. For they may prophesy, as is granted, Mt. 7. But I call this revelation ineffectual because they may be castaways for all this. But properly, revelation is the heritage of the saints. For in them only it is effectual, and thus the Lord does grant revelation in two degrees: 1. Sometimes it is such an illumination as works a full assurance: sometimes it is an illumination that works only a persuasion. In weak Christians the work of the Spirit of revelation is persuasion, but in strong Christians it is full assurance.

t:
A second question is, How far the Law can draw a sinner to Christ? Antinomians tell us of a legal drawing and conversion, and of an evangelic drawing; the legal drawing they say is ours [that of the reformed]; the latter theirs. Assertion 1. The difference between the letter of the Law and the Gospel is not in the manner of working, for the letter of either Law or Gospel is alike ineffectual and fruitless to draw any to Christ. Christ preached the Gospel to hard-hearted Pharisees; it moved them not. Moses preached the Law and the curses thereof to the stiffnecked Jews and they were as little humbled. Sounds and syllables of ten hells, of twenty heavens and Gospels, without the Spirit’s working, are alike fruitless. And we grant the Law is a sleepy keeper of a captive sinner; he may either steal away from his keeper or if he be awed with his keeper, he is not kept from any spiritual, internal breach of the Law, nor moved thereby to sincere and spiritual walking. But the difference between Law and Gospel is not in the internal manner of working, but in two other things:

1. In the matter contained in Law and Gospel: because nature is refractory to violence and the Law can do nothing but curse sinners; therefore it can draw no man to Christ. The Gospel again contains sweet and glorious promises of giving a new heart to the elect, of admitting to the Prince of peace laden and broken-hearted mourners in Zion and in conferring on them a free imputed righteousness; and this is in itself a taking-way, but without the Gospel-spirit [it is] utterly ineffectual.

2. To the Gospel there is a Spirit added, which works as God does with an omnipotent pull; and this Spirit does also use the Law to prepare and humble; though this be by a higher power than goes along with the Law as the Law.

t: Question 9. Whether every will of God is fulfilled? Denied with a distinction. Answer: Concerning the will properly taken, or of good-pleasure [beneplaciti]: affirmed, Isa. 46:10. Concerning the will taken metonymically, or of command [mandati]: denied. And this opinion is insinuated by Thomas, in [Summa] pt. 1, question 19, article 6, where he disputes that every will of God is always fulfilled, together with article 11, where he distinguishes the will into [the will] of the sign and [the will] of good-pleasure. … Question 11. By what will can anyone justly will that which God does not will? Explained. Answer: We thus explain it: by a right will, which is conformable to the law and general command of God, one can will that which God does not will by the will of good-pleasure, or the hidden [will]. See Gen. 22, compared with Heb. 11:17 and 2 Sam. 7:2-3, 13. Question 12, Whether the precepts of God sometimes differ from his will? Affirmed with a distinction. Answer: In the proximate object they differ: for of the precept, or command, there can be another object—and indeed an opposite one—than [that] of the will or good-pleasure. As is manifest, Gen. 22, where the proximate object of the divine command given to Abraham was the slaying [mactatio] of Isaac; and the object of the good-pleasure, or of the divine will properly so called, was the non-slaying of the same. But although the objects of the will of command and of good-pleasure are opposed among themselves, yet the acts of command and of will are not opposed, but the former is subordinated to the latter. For God, by the will of good-pleasure, willed the command, or to command Abraham; but He did not will the thing commanded to Abraham, or the fulfillment of the commanded thing.

359. XI. The next distinction of God’s will is into effectual and uneffectual. And here he that would see a great deal said on the question, Whether God have any uneffectual will, and whether man’s will can frustrate it, may see too much in a multitude of Schoolmen on [Lombard] Sentences, dist. 1, quest. 45 & 46.¹ ¹ Aquinas, art. 1; Scotus, quest. unica; Durandus, quest. 1; Bonaventura, art. 1; Gregory Ariminiensis, quest. unica, art. 3; Pennot. bk. 4, ch. 22; Alvarez, De Auxiliis, disp. 32; Ruiz, De Voluntate, disp. 18; Granada, Of the Will of God, tract. 4, disp. 3; Suarez, bk. 4, Of Predestination, ch. 8; Gregory Valencia, disp. 1, quest. 19, p. 6; Cajetan; Nazar. Ban. Zum. Navar. Gonzal. Molina; Vasquez, etc. in [Aquinas, Summa] pt. 1, quest. 19, art. 6; Ripa. Arrub. Fasol. ibid.; Nic. D’Orbel., pt. 1, dist. 46 and many other Scotists, etc. Some answer (as D’Orbellis, etc.) that the voluntas beneplaciti [will of good-pleasure] is ever effectual, but not the voluntas signi; which yet seeing he well explains to be only the making of duty, he might well have said is still effectual to its proper primary effect. Gregory Ariminiensis (and many others) distinguish of the will of complacency and displicency, and that prosecutionis et fugae; and say the latter is effectual and not the former: which others say of the absolute will as distinct from the conditional. The plain truth I have oft opened before: God’s will is the first efficient, the chief dirigent and the final cause (in which the three principles, power, wisdom and goodness are eminent).

1. His efficient will is ever effectual and never frustrated. ‘Whatsoever pleased the Lord (to do) that He did in heaven and in earth, in the sea and in the depths.’ Ps. 135:6. ‘And who has resisted (this) his will?’ Rom. 9:19.

2. His directing will is ever effectual as to the making of the Law or rule, and of due or right thereby: For so far it is efficient of that effect: But it is too oft violated by our sin.

3. His final will or complacency, is God’s being pleased with the being, or action, or relation of the creature, and supposing it, [it] is not efficient [because it is an end, final goal], and therefore [it is] not effectual. And I know no need of more upon this question.

t: God’s call sometimes is ineffectual, and sometimes effectual. So the same apostle plainly declares in 1 Thess. 2:13: “For this cause also thank we God, which effectually works also in you that believe.” Observe that it is the work of God’s Spirit in the heart, superadded to the Word of the Gospel, as spoken by men, that makes any call effectual. Without this inward work, God may call, and the soul will never answer… It is this effectual work of God’s Spirit, in regenerating the soul by infusing of habits of grace, which distinguishes an internal effectual call of God form a mere external and ineffectual one… The text makes sure that it might be known whether or not God has so called you by His Word, as that also He has worked in you by His Spirit; whether God has illuminated your understanding, and inclined your will, so that you have complied with God’s will, and have answered His call. Whether, when God drew you, you ran after Him (Cant. 1:4); whether, when God entreated and persuaded you to be reconciled to Him you consented (2 Cor. 5:20); whether, when He wooed you, He also won you; whether, when He invited you to the wedding supper of His Son, you made no excuse or delay, but accepted, and welcomed the offer of the Gospel with faith and love (Luke 14:18). All which if you did do, it arose from the power of an inward call, being superadded to the outward call of the Word…

Three things are to be observed in this speech:

1. God’s resolution not always to strive with man by his Spirit. My Spirit has striven a great while; it shall strive yet a little longer; but it shall not strive always. The Holy Spirit is a striving Spirit with the children of men; striving them away from sin, and to bring them to God; striving by the checks of their own consciences, but the ministry of the Word, by the rebukes of Providence; striving by one fair warning after another to reclaim the sinner. Have not we ourselves experienced these strivings?—something within us that has whispered in an hour of temptation, “Do not this abominable thing which the Lord hates?” ‘Twill be our wisdom to hearken to such whispers, and to close with them, striving against sin. Heb 12:4. If the Spirit of God be resisted in its strivings, and quenched in its motions, though it may strive long, yet it will not strive always. ‘Tis a principle with men not to be always persuading those with whom they cannot prevail; neither will the blessed Spirit do so. If Ephraim be joined to idols, is it not a righteous thing with God to say, Strive no more with him, let him alone? Hosea 4:17. What guest will stay long there where he is not welcome? Is it not wisdom then to improve these strivings while we have them?

2. The reason of that resolution: For that he also is flesh; carnal, earthly, sensual, corrupted, depraved, defiled; and therefore ‘tis to no purpose to strive with him; ‘tis but labor lost. It is as good to go about to change the Ethiopian’s skin or the leopard’s spots, as to reclaim and reform these impenitent sinners. Flesh, in scripture, is frequently opposed to spirit. It is the corrupt nature that renders the strivings of the blessed Spirit ineffectual. ‘Tis the law in the members that wars against the law of the mind. Rom. 7:23. The flesh and the spirit are sworn enemies one to another, and between them there is a constant conflict. Gal. 5:17. Now where the flesh, the carnal part, is so far suffered to prevail, as that the man may be denominated flesh, there the Spirit will not always, will not long strive. Those therefore that would enjoy the Spirit’s strivings, must curb and restrain, and not gratify and encourage, the corrupt motions and carnal desires of the flesh and of the mind. Eph. 2:3.

t: This comes in here as a token of God’s displeasure at those who married strange wives; He threatens to withdraw from them his Spirit, whom they had grieved by such marriages, contrary to their convictions: fleshly lusts are often punished with spiritual judgments, the sorest of all judgments. Or as another occasion of the great wickedness of the old world; the Spirit of the Lord, being provoked by their resistance of his motions, ceased to strive with them, and then all religion was soon lost among them. This He warns them of before, that they might not further vex his Holy Spirit, but by their prayers might stay Him with them. Observe in this verse, I. God’s resolution not always to strive with man by his Spirit. The Spirit then strove by Noah’s preaching (1 Pt. 3:19–20) and by inward checks, but it was in vain with the most of men; therefore, says God, He shall not always strive. Note, 1. The blessed Spirit strives with sinners, by the convictions and admonitions of conscience, to turn them from sin to God. If the Spirit be resisted, quenched, and striven against, though He strive long, he will not strive always, Hos. 4:17. Those are ripening apace for ruin whom the Spirit of grace has left off striving with. II. The reason of this resolution: For that he also is flesh, that is, incurably corrupt, and carnal, and sensual, so that it is labor lost to strive with him. Can the Ethiopian change his skin? He also, that is, All, one as well as another, they have all sunk into the mire of flesh. Note, 1. It is the corrupt nature, and the inclination of the soul towards the flesh, that oppose the Spirit’s strivings and render them ineffectual. When a sinner has long adhered to that interest, and sided with the flesh against the Spirit, the Spirit justly withdraws his agency, and strives no more. None lose the Spirit’s strivings but those that have first forfeited them.

t: 13. In the same way too it cannot be concluded that because the outward calling of the rejected is ineffectual it is therefore not seriously meant by God. Outward calling is always per se [of itself, in principle] a real calling to salvation, since everyone who follows it up thereby gains righteousness in Christ and eternal life: only, in the case of the godless, it is ineffectual because of their hardness of heart. Similarly, the calling from God’s side is always seriously intended, since God promises grace even to the rejected upon condition of faith, and makes faith for them a duty. But of course God omits to give faith to the rejected, because He is not bound to do so in the case of any man… From this it follows that even the calling of the godless is on God’s side ‘sincere and serious’.

For God’s mercy being actio sublevantis [an act of taking away] and not passio condolentis [a passion of suffering with], it ties Him not to do all He can for redeeming any man out of his misery; but his action is ordered and limited by his own free-will. It is the height and riches of God’s mercy which from everlasting has prepared for the elect only, and in time bestows upon them only that special and effectual grace which infallibly brings them unto glory. t: XXV. Thirdly, it is asked how Christ could offer such prayers to God as openly appear to be repugnant to the divine counsel and will, and thus to the piety and obedience which he most constantly exhibited to the Father? For what? Was he not born and made mediator for this very reason, that he might drink this cup for our salvation? Did he not know that this was the decree of the Father, as he himself testified more than once, that he must suffer many things and be killed? Mt. 16:21. Indeed, when he was being seized by the soldiers, he rebukes Peter for resisting them: “Shall I not drink the cup which my Father hath given me?” How, therefore, is he contrary to himself and to the Father, by requesting with such effort that the cup be transferred from him? Here, indeed, there are many things that can be replied. 1st, We suppose, against the Monothelites, that there was a twofold will in Christ, just as there was a divine and a human nature; these were not indeed adverse and repugnant to one another, but were nevertheless diverse insofar as they were directed toward diverse objects. The divine [will] willed death because it had been so ordained by the Father for our redemption; the human, however, shuddered and prayed against it, because it viewed it as the destruction of nature and the most dire of all evils that could exist; yet the human will is not rightly said to have been repugnant to the divine, because it petitioned not absolutely, but conditionally; not with a deliberate and elective will, but rather with an inefficacious and natural velleity. Therefore, it is to be observed 2nd, that the will can be divided in many ways; for one is called efficacious, another inefficacious; that is called efficacious which is the principle of acting, and which moves and impels a man to execute those things which it wills and to remove, as much as it can, any impediments to operation; [Ineffectual] which is not brought into effect, whether because of impediments arriving from elsewhere, or because it is a simple complacency in the good, or displeasure at evil, and does not proceed further so as to be a principle of operating, nor does it in reality impel one to the execution of the thing, which deserves to be called velleity rather than will. Therefore, when Christ is said to have willed that the cup might pass, this ought not to be understood of an efficacious will which produced in Him any attempt at escaping and extricating Himself from those snares; indeed, we see Him led as a sheep to the slaughter, Isa. LIII:8, so that He in no way resisted, nor attempted to flee from death, but of an ineffectual will which signifies nothing other than a simple displeasure arising from a natural inclination by which the will abhors that which destroys nature. XXVI. The will is either natural and indeliberate, or deliberate and elective. The former is called will by way of nature, the latter by way of reason, thus Thomas, pt. 3, quest. 18, art. 5. Will as nature, or by way of nature, is a physical faculty having a natural inclination toward the preservation of the whole composite, or it is a desire for advantage; it is called indeliberate will because it is borne toward an object considered absolutely without any consideration of circumstances. But will by way of reason is a rational faculty for pursuing the general good of the whole man as he is man, or for following the dictate of the practical intellect advising what is right and just; it is called elective will because it is a desire and affection for justice rather than for one’s own utility; it is also called deliberate will because it regards an object clothed in all its circumstances, and this will is referred to rational cognition as to its cause, because it follows not the instinct of nature but the dictate of reason. The will of nature naturally flees those things which are contrary to nature, such as death, torments, etc. The will by way of reason can be borne even toward those things which are adverse to nature, provided they are just and honorable or necessary; thus, for example, he who by natural will flees and is averse to a bitter potion, nevertheless receives the same by rational will, because he knows there is no other way of recovering health. In the same way, martyrs by nature cannot but shudder at death, but the same persons, nevertheless, approach it eagerly out of reason as the most glorious testimony of the benevolence of God, and glory in it. In clearly the same manner, Christ willed and did not will death, in a different respect. The will by way of nature did not will it, but the same by way of reason willed it; it did not will it insofar as natural appetite was a desire that He might live, and it viewed death absolutely and in itself as the destruction of nature. But insofar as He viewed the same with its circumstances, that is, as decreed by God and necessary for the salvation of the elect, He was borne toward it with a most propense affection, just as He testified elsewhere that this was His food, that He might do the will of His Father. Jn. IV:34; XXVII:4. Will is distinguished into simple and absolute, and hypothetical or conditional. The former is that by which one wills something absolutely and efficaciously, so that he leaves nothing undone so that that will may be brought into effect. The latter in which one wills something under a condition, and which is contained within certain limits. Thus, with an absolute will, the faithful seek the remission of their sins, and whatever things are necessary for their salvation. But with a conditional will, they seek those things which do not pertain to salvation in themselves, nor, whether granted, promote it, or, if denied, remove it—for instance, wealth, health, strength, external peace—in the seeking of which they must always add that condition, expressly or implicitly: “if the will of God so carries it.

t:
XXXII. Finally, it is asked here how Christ can be said to have been heard in that prayer from fear, as the apostle testifies, Heb. V:7 [“Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared;”], and elsewhere Christ professes that he is always heard by the Father, Jn. XI:42, when nevertheless death had necessarily to be undergone by him. That which Christ willed simply and absolutely, in that he never suffered a refusal; but that which he willed only under a condition, it is no wonder if he did not obtain it, since that was not so much a will as it was velleity, and that was not so much to be reckoned a rational desire, which ought always to hold the primary place, as a natural inclination and sensitive appetite, which never has the principal role in prayer. 2. Christ was heard from the fear of death, not indeed absolutely, as if He had been freed from the necessity of undergoing death, but in a certain respect, namely, insofar as God, who heard Him, so shook off that fear that He received death most steadfastly and submitted Himself wholly to the divine will, and was thus strengthened so that He laid aside all dread of death. For Christ feared two things above all:

1. Lest He should succumb, overwhelmed by the evils which He saw to be most grievous.

2. Lest He should be swallowed up by death, so that no exit from it would be open. But God heard Him, that is, freed Him from both those fears:

1. Because He so corroborated Him by the power of His Spirit in the midst of the struggle that He most steadfastly and invincibly sustained that most grievous contest.

2. Because He freed Him from death, having loosed the pains of hell by His glorious resurrection; and thus, most truly, in this respect He was heard—not, indeed, that He might not pay the penalty of death, but that He might not be swallowed up by it; not that He might not taste it, but that He might not perish in it; not in the subterfuge of punishments, but in the constant toleration of the same and in a strong and invincible liberation and victory.

t: As God may by metaphor be said to will what by His will, properly speaking, He wills not; so He may by metaphor be said to will what He does will, properly speaking. Hence there is nothing to prevent the same thing being the object of the will of good pleasure and of the will of expression [sign]. But operation is always the same as the will of good pleasure; while precept and counsel are not; both because the former regards the present, and the two latter the future; and because the former is of itself the effect of the will; the latter its effect as fulfilled by means of another.
w: Summa, pt. 1

t:
Section 4, ‘On the imperfections which an inefficacious will and a will suspended from a condition seem to display: objections are dissolved.’ .

1. Certain arguments of the contrary opinion have been solved elsewhere, or will have to be solved below; for certain arguments are directed immediately to proving that the divine will totally precedes our wills, so that in no way does it wait for them. But these have been solved elsewhere. Other arguments, however, contend immediately and directly that the application of God to concur with free choice would be confused, blind, and fortuitous, if it were to depend on a condition, provided that free choice should will. Nevertheless we shall show this inference to be null below in disputation 45 and the following.

2. But the following objections seem to be proper to the present undertaking. The first is: Inefficacy of will is an imperfection; therefore no will of God is inefficacious. It is confirmed, because the desire of a thing not to be obtained by its nature is apt to sadden and afflict the one desiring. It is answered: Inefficacy is an imperfection when it proceeds from impotence of the will. But when the will could, if it willed, effectively obtain any object whatsoever, and yet does not will to obtain it effectively, but only to desire it ineffectively; then rather it is a perfection of the will, and a dominion over itself and over its power. It is confirmed, since to will not to produce other worlds is not an imperfection, but rather a perfection; therefore likewise to will not to produce effectively free actions, but only to supply to them a sufficient concurrence, will not be an imperfection. To the confirmation it is answered: if the desired thing is not obtained on account of a defect of power, or if the desired thing increases in some way the happiness of the desiring will; then not to obtain that thing can of itself sadden and afflict. But to God neither is there lacking power to obtain, nor is the happiness of God increased in anyway by the obtaining of the desired thing.

3. The second objection is, that: A conditional volition is proper to a will which cannot obtain that good without the condition appended: just as a conditional will of retaining wares in a storm [on the sea] is proper to a will which cannot avoid shipwreck unless a jettison of the wares be made. It is confirmed, because that will of the merchant would effectively preserve the wares, if he could without danger, or inconvenience, and difficulty. But God, without danger, inconvenience, and difficulty, could have saved all men, if He willed. Therefore neither by a conditional will does He will their salvation.

4. It is answered: By denying the first antecedent. For although the will be omnipotent, and can without an appended condition obtain such a good, nonetheless most wisely and most powerfully it uses a conditioned volition, when another greater good, incompatible, is loved by an efficacious volition, which depends on the aforesaid condition. But the [proposed] greater good is a better administration of the universe, and a more illustrious manifestation of divine justice together with mercy requires that the salvation of all be loved, as much as regards God, efficaciously; nor does it allow that, by the antecedent will of God, impediments of salvation be decreed and procured; yet at the same time it requires that many men be so left to their own choice that they be permitted, if they will, to resist the aforesaid will of God. Since therefore this greater good efficaciously willed by God implies a contradiction with the salvation of those same men efficaciously willed, for that reason God most wisely and most powerfully appends a condition to His will, depending upon the choice of men. For this volition satisfies the natural propensity and benevolence, which He professes toward men, even the reprobate, without dissimulation. It is confirmed: By the example of the human will of Christ the Lord, to whom there was not lacking the power of avoiding death, according to that of Mt. 26: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and He will provide for Me now more than twelve legions of angels?” and Jn. 10: “I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from Me; but I lay it down of Myself.
w: Commentaries & Disputations on the First Part of St. Thomas, on the Will of God & its Proper Acts

t: …the worship of God is twofold, inward or outward… The outward is that worship whereby the inward is testified outwardly in the speach and actions… Indeed all the worship of God is spiritual, even that which we call outward; yet not of itself, but by virtue of the inward, from which it proceeds. The heads of inward worship are two: adoration of God and cleaving to God… Now in adoration there are four virtues: feare, obedience, patience, thankfulness. … The second virtue of adoration is inward obedience of the hidden man of the heart. The Lord prefers this obedience before all sacrifice, 1 Sam. 15:22. This stands in two things. First, in yielding subjection of the conscience to the commandments, threatnings and promises of God, so as we are willing that it should become bound unto them. Secondly, when the rest of the powers of the soul, in their place and time, perform obedience unto God. … …touching inward worship, we must remember that it alone is properly, simply, and of itself, the worship of God; and the outward is not simply the worship of God, but only so far forth as it is quickened by the inward, and grounded upon it.
w: The Whole Treatise of the Cases of Conscience

t: He certainly did not suspect the Corinthians of such a degree of ignorance or carelessness as to think that they worshipped idols in their heart. But as they made no scruple of frequenting the assemblies of the wicked, and observing along with them certain rites instituted in honor of idols, he condemns this liberty taken by them, as being a very bad example. It is certain, then, that when he here makes mention of idolatry, he, speaks of what is outward, or, if you prefer it, of the profession of idolatry. For as God is said to be worshipped by the bending of the knee, and other tokens of reverence, while the principal and genuine worship of Him is inward, so is it also as to idols, for the case holds the same in things opposite. It is to no purpose that very many in the present day endeavor to excuse outward actions on this pretext, that the heart is not in them, while Paul convicts of idolatry those very acts, and assuredly with good reason. For, as we owe to God not merely the secret affection of the heart, but also outward adoration, the man who offers to an idol an appearance of adoration takes away so much of the honor due to God. Let him allege as he may that his heart is quite away from it. The action itself is to be seen, in which the honor that is due to God is transferred to an idol.
w: Commentary on 1 Corinthians

t:
5. Divine worship is internal only or external also. Internal worship is merely spiritual, and performed only within the temple of man’s heart, of which none are witnesses but God and a man’s own conscience. All the inward motions of the heart directed unto God are parts of this worship, as faith, hope, confidence, love, fear and joy in God, etc. which are all of them diverse acts and parts of inward worship, in everyone of which God is honored. All which spring from the apprehension of our own wants, and God’s infinite excellency and goodness towards us…

6. External worship is an expressing and setting forth of the internal by outward signs and rites: by which as by certain outward bodily shadows and colors the spiritual and inward worship of God is made visible and sensible to others.
w: A Treatise of Divine Worship

t: …it lies as a necessary duty upon all to worship and serve God. The Hebrew words and Greek are several and observable that express this worship, which are exactly handled among the learned; The ground of this worship is because He is the Jehovah, who giveth us our being, and all other mercies: It is therefore most natural and a most indispensable debt to acknowledge Him for his supreme excellency herein and to give Him a peculiar and proper worship. Now this worship and service is either internal, or external, or mixed, compounded of both; internal consists in our love of God above all things, faith and hope in Him, obedience to his commands, which the Scripture prefers before all external worship; External is that of adoration and inclination of the body, kissing the hand, bowing the knee, dedicating temples, altars, and offering of sacrifices; Mixed is compounded of both these, such as calling upon God’s name by petition and thanksgiving.
w: Spiritual Refining: or A Treatise of Grace and Assurance

t: For principally and properly God is worshipped in our spirit: Jn. 4:24, ‘The true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit.’ Rom. 1:9, ‘Whom I serve in my spirit.’ 1 Pet. 3:15, ‘Sanctify God in your hearts.’ By the ‘spirit’ I understand the thought of the mind, the consience and the affections of the heart. For in these is the first and principal seat of divine and spiritual worship. As for the body, it is but a secondary instrument of the service of God… the true religion of the New Testament has but few prescribed ceremonies and for the most part is divine and spiritual.

Moreover, being severed from inward worship, it is worship in show, and not worship in truth. If they eye be evil, the whole body is dark. (Mt. 6:13) Christ bids the Pharisees to wash the inside of the cup and platter, and then all shall be clean (Mt. 23:25-26).

t: On the other hand [in contrast to Christianity], those who introduced the errors of the sects proceeded in contrary fashion, as is clear from Mohammed, who enticed peoples with the promise of carnal pleasures, to the desire of which the concupiscence of the flesh instigates. He also delivered commandments in keeping with his promises, by giving the reins to carnal pleasure, in which it is easy for carnal men to obey. Also, the lessons of truth which he inculcated were only such as can be easily known to any man of average wisdom by his natural powers—in fact, he mingled the truths which he taught with many fables and most false doctrines. Nor did he add any signs of supernatural agency, which alone are a fitting witness to divine inspiration, since a visible work that can only be from God proves the teacher of truth to be invisibly inspired, but he asserted that he was sent in the power of arms, which sign is not lacking even to robbers and tyrants. Again, those who believed in him from the outset were not wise men practiced in things divine and human, but bestial men who dwelt in the deserts, utterly ignorant of all divine teaching, and it was by a multitude of such men and the force of arms that he compelled others to submit to his law. Lastly, no divine oracles of prophets in a previous age bore witness to him; rather, he corrupted almost all the teaching of the Old and New Testaments by a narrative replete with fables, as one may see by a perusal of his law. Hence, by a cunning device, he did not commit the reading of the Old and New Testament books to his followers, lest he should thereby be convicted of falsehood. Thus it is evident that those who believe his words believe lightly.
w: Summa Contra Gentiles

t: First, we need to keep in mind the Fregean point that a difference in sense does not entail a difference in reference. To use Frege’s famous example, the sense of the expression “the morning star” is different from the sense of the expression “the evening star.” But these two expressions refer to one and the same thing, viz. the planet Venus. Similarly, expressions like “the God of the Christians” and “the God of the Muslims” differ in sense, but it doesn’t follow from that alone that they don’t refer to the same God… Second, even a speaker’s erroneous beliefs don’t entail that he is not referring to the same thing that speakers with correct beliefs are referring to… Similarly, the fact that Muslims have what Christians regard as a number of erroneous beliefs about God does not by itself entail that Muslims and Christians are not referring to the same thing when they use the expression “God.
w: ‘Christians, Muslims & the Reference of ‘God”

t: In the religion of the Mahumetans I find much good, viz. a confession of one only God, and most of the natural parts of religion; a vehement opposition to all idolatry; a testimony to the veracity of Moses, and of Christ; that Christ is the Word of God, and a great prophet, and the writings of the apostles true: All this therefore where Christianity is approved, must be embraced. And there is no doubt but God has made use of Mahumet as a great scourge to the idolaters of the world; as well as to the Christians who had abused their sacred privileges and blessings: Wherever his religion does prevail, he casts down images, and fills men’s minds with a hatred of idols, and all conceit of multitude of Gods, and brings men to worship one God alone, and does that by the sword in this, which the preaching of the Gospel had not done in many obstinate nations of idolaters.
w: The Reasons of the Christian Religion

t: In reality there are two, and only two, foundations of law; and they are both of them conditions without which nothing can give it any force; I mean equity and utility. With respect to the former, it grows out of the great rule of equality, which is grounded upon our common nature, and which Philo, with propriety and beauty, calls the mother of justice. All human laws are, properly speaking, only declaratory; they may alter the mode and application, but have no power over the substance of original justice. The other foundation of law, which is utility, connected in the same manner with, and derived directly from, our rational nature; for any other utility may be the utility of a robber, but cannot be that of a citizen; the interest of the domestic enemy, and not that of a member of the commonwealth. This present equality can never be the foundation of statues which create an artificial difference between men, as the laws before us [under consideration in his time] do, in order to induce a consequential inequality in the distribution of justice. Law is a mode of human action respecting society, and must be governed by the same rules of equity which govern every private action; and so Tully [Cicero?] considers it in his Offices as the only utility [being a utility to all commonly] agreeable to that [common] nature…

Wiki: “His first published work was A Discourse… This appeared in 1648, probably in July at the height of the political uncertainty engendered by the second Civil War. The previous month the Army had shown that it wielded both political and military power and Ascham’s Discourse was widely seen as a defense of the Army as the conquering power, and as a plea for “the rank of the people” to adopt a position of political quiescence. Parliament’s ultimate victory and the establishment of the Commonwealth posed a problem for those who felt unable to accept the legality of the new government but were now being required to give it their allegiance, and also for those who regarded their oath of allegiance to King Charles I… as a solemn oath to God that could not be broken. One argument, provided by a group of political theorists variously called the Engagers, or de facto theorists, was to argue that an individual could give their obedience to the de facto government in being simply because it was in power. For many such a theory was deeply shocking since it emphasized power at the expense of authority, and subordinated allegiance to self-interest. The debate was initiated by Francis Rous who published a brief pamphlet in April 1649 [The Lawfulness of Obeying the Present Government] in which he argued that allegiance could be given to the Commonwealth even though it were acknowledged to be an illegal power. It was a radical shift in the basis of the argument that was to be followed through by theorists engaged in the debate on de facto government. In the debate that followed Ascham played a major part in developing a theory of political obligation to the de facto power. In 1649 it is possible that he was author of a short anonymous pamphlet, A Combate between Two Seconds. One for Obeying the Present Government. The Other the second part of a Demurrer undeservedly called Religious, which was published in July. This work firstly took issue with those whose arguments continued to be based on Romans 13:1–2 and in particular addressed the arguments in an anonymous work that may have been published in two parts, but that is extant only in its second part entitled The Second Part of the Religious Demurrer; and secondly bypassed the critical emphasis on Romans 13:1–2 to develop arguments based on the need to protect oneself from chaos, as originally deployed by Ascham in his 1648 Discourse. Having thus entered the pamphlet “war”, Ascham then began to expand his arguments. He was certainly the author of a longer pamphlet, The Bounds and Bonds of Publique Obedience, which appeared in August 1649; and by November he had added nine chapters to his 1648 Discourse, which now appeared under the title Of the Confusions and Revolutions of Government. This work attracted the attention of Robert Sanderson who criticized it in a short and pungent pamphlet [Resolutions of Conscience (by a learned Divine) in answer to a letter sent with Mr. Ascham’s Book, Treating, How farre it may be lawful to submit to an Usurped Power.]. Ascham’s Reply to a paper of Dr. Sanderson’s, containing a censure of Mr. A. A. his book of the Confusions and Revolution of Government, which was published on 9 January 1650, was directed as much as against Edward Gee‘s Exercitation concerning usurped powers as against Sanderson’s work. In these works Ascham’s essential argument was that in a situation in which people had to look after their own safety, they were justified in giving their allegiance to any power that was capable of protecting them, whatever the legality of its title to power. By the autumn of 1649 the debate began to center on the specific question of the Oath of Allegiance and the Engagement to the Commonwealth: Two Acts of Parliament were passed requiring people to take an Oath of Allegiance to the Commonwealth, on 11/12 October 1649, and on 2 January 1650. Conventionally oaths were regarded as “the strictest ties and obligations that a man can be under”. For many the Engagement to the Commonwealth was impossible to take because it overrode their prior obligation to the monarchy (King Charles I and his heirs). The Presbyterian Richard Baxter held that he “could not judge it seemly for him that believed there is a God to play fast and loose with a dreadful oath”. (Reliquiae Baxterianae, London, 1696, p. 54) In contrast, Ascham argued that all oaths involved tacit conditions, of which the ability of the government to protect the people was the main one. A government that could not protect its people lost the right to their allegiance. Ascham’s 1648 Discourse was to be republished, anonymously, following the ousting of King James II [in 1688/9]. Then the question of the legality of the oath of allegiance to King William and Queen Mary [in the Glorious Revolution] had come to the fore. It did not, however, generate any discussion. By then the leading theorist in the field was Thomas Hobbes, whose De Corpore Politico, De Cive (first edition), and Leviathan, had systematized a coherent and secular defense of the contract as between ruler and ruled.
w: A Discourse

(d. 1676; n.p., n.d.) Hale (1609-1676) was an Anglican and influential barrister, judge and jurist most noted for his treatise, The History of the Pleas of the Crown. Hale’s early works, including, A Discourse of the Knowledge of God, reflect his early Puritan and Reformed background. After ca. 1660 his thought becomes more Arminian. Hale’s Analysis of the Common Law (below) is noted as the first published history of English law and a strong influence on William Blackstone’s Commentaries on the Laws of England. Hale’s jurisprudence struck a middle-ground between Edward Coke’s “appeal to reason” and John Selden’s “appeal to contract”, while refuting elements of Thomas Hobbes’s theory of natural law. In 1662, as a judge, though it was required of him, he refused to declare the National Covenant and the Solemn League & Covenant to be unlawful oaths. The work above shows influences from Stair’s philosophical training, his foreign travels, and continental jurists as well as English lawyers. In 1695 there was published a small volume entitled, A Vindication of the Divine Perfections, Illustrating the Glory of God in them by Reason and Revelation, methodically digested… It is undoubtedly Stair’s work, and was edited by the two Nonconformist divines, William Bates and John Howe. . 1700’s See below on Common Law & English law. . 1800’s Thomas, John Penford – A Treatise of Universal Jurisprudence (London, 1829) ToC Bastiat, Frederic – The Law (1850; NY: 1964) Bastiat (1801–1850) was a French economist, writer and a prominent member of the French Liberal School. A Freemason and a member of the French National Assembly, Bastiat developed the economic concept of opportunity cost. As an advocate of classical economics and the economics of Adam Smith, his views favored a free market and influenced the Austrian School. Bastiat did most of his writing during the years just before — and immediately following — the Revolution of February 1848. This was the period when France was rapidly turning to complete socialism. As a Deputy to the Legislative Assembly, Bastiat was studying and explaining each socialist fallacy as it appeared. And he explained how socialism must inevitably degenerate into communism. But most of his countrymen chose to ignore his logic. t: § 10, Direction 7. Meddle not with lawsuits till you have offered an equal arbitration of indifferent men, or used all possible means of love to prevent them. Lawsuits are not the first, but the last remedy. Try all others before you use them. § 11, Direction 8. When you must needs go to law, compose your minds to unfeigned love towards him that you must contend with, and watch over your hearts with suspicion and the strictest care, lest secret disaffection get advantage by it; And go to your neighbor and labor to possess his heart also with love, and to demulce [pacify] his mind, that you may not use the courts of justice as soldiers do their weapons, to do the worst they can against another, as an enemy: but as loving friends do use an amicable arbitration, resolving contentedly to stand to what the judge determines, without any alienation of mind or abatement of brotherly love. § 12, Direction 9. Be not too confident of the righteousness of your own cause, but ask counsel of some understanding, godly and impartial men; and hear all that can be said, and patiently consider of the case, and do as you would have others do by you.

t: Question 8: May a guilty person plead not guilty, or deny the fact? Answer: Common use is the interpreter of words: If the common use of those words does make their public sense a lie, it may not be done. But if the forensic [legal] common use of the denial is taken to signify no more but this, ‘Let him that accuses me, prove it’ [then]: I am not bound to accuse my self, or, in foro [in court] I am not guilty till it be proved, then it is lawful to plead ‘not-guilty’ and deny the fact, except in cases wherein you are bound to an open confession, or in which the scandal will do more hurt than the denial will do good.

t: Only thus much I should advise, that if it be known that any person is guilty of a capital crime (as for example of adultery) though we be not bound alway to accuse them openly, or to bring them to such a confession or self-accusation as may hazard their lives, yet: 1. The pastor may suspend them and in some cases require the people to avoid them when the fact is publicly known (though the party not prosecuted) and give but a general intimation of the fault, as known already; though perhaps the evidence will not hold in law. (As I have known persons that openly confess adultery at home, but denying it before the judge, come off as if they were innocent; and yet confess it again when they come home.) And I should think that such persons should not be re-admitted to Communion, till they do manifest public serious penitence in the congregation: but only in general terms (seeing they are not bound to accuse themselves, so as to expose their lives to danger), as thus: ‘I confess before God and this congregation that I am a heinous sinner, and unworthy of communion with the Church: the particulars I need not express, seeing the congregation may easily know my meaning, etc.'

Question 9: Is a man ever bound to accuse himself, and seek justice against himself? Answer 1: In many cases a man is bound to punish himself: As when the law against swearing, cursing or the like, does give the poor a certain mulct [fine] which is the penalty: He ought to give that money himself: And in cases where it is a necessary cure to himself: And in any case where the public good requires it: As if a magistrate offend whom none else will punish, or who is the judge in his own cause: he should so far punish himself as is necessary to the suppression of sin, and to the preserving of the honor of the laws: As I have heard of a justice that swore twenty oaths, and paid his twenty shillings for it.

2. A man may be bound in such a divine vengeance or judgment as seeks after his particular sin, to offer himself to be a sacrifice to justice, to stop the judgement: As Jonah and Achan did.

3. A man may be bound to confess his guilt and offer himself to justice to save the innocent, who is falsely accused and condemned for his crime.

4. But in ordinary cases a man is not bound to be his own public accuser or executioner. Question 10: May a witness voluntarily speak that truth which he knows will further an unrighteous cause, and be made use of to oppress the innocent? Answer: He may never do it as a confederate in that intention: Nor may he do it when he knows that it will tend to such an event (though threatened or commanded) except when some weightier accident does preponderate for the doing it (as the avoiding of a greater hurt to others than it will bring on the oppressed, etc.). Question 11: May a witness conceal some part of the truth? Answer: Not when he swears to deliver the whole truth: nor when a good cause is like[ly] to suffer, or a bad cause to be furthered by the concealment: nor when he is under any other obligation to reveal the whole.

t: Assertion 4. There may be some cases in which it is expedient to admit an accuser, and not to admit a process without one. As suppose one were under no ill report and yet some gross scandal were imputed to him, which were not of such fame, or had not such presumptions as to give ground for a Church-judicatory immediately to interpose, and the scandal being of such a nature as the trial thereof could neither be omitted, nor closed in private; in that case, suppose one should complain of the Church’s negligence in the same, asserting the evidences to be clear, and offering to make them out; In such a case, I say, the Church can hardly refuse to hear him, lest they be thought partial; nor is there ground, nor is it fit for them immediately to pursue it: Therefore an accuser is expedient, that so, upon the one side, the Church’s impartiality may be vindicated in refusing the complaint of no sober man, nor the uttermost of any trial, that in well grounded reason they may expect; And, on the other side, that the mouths of some needless and too importunate complainers may be stopped, and they themselves found censurable, if either without cause they traduce the Church-officers as negligent and partial, while there is access to make out before them such a truth if it be truth; or if precipitantly and inconsiderately (if not maliciously) they have tabled a scandal against another as a public scandal which they cannot make out, and so have needlessly troubled a Church-judicatory in such a matter and sinfully wronged their neighbor. For, a process in such cases where it cannot be made out, is scandalous: therefore if a person rest not satisfied so as to abstain till he have trial put to the utmost, he is to be dealt with as a scandalous person, lest men take liberty, under the pretext of pursuing offences, to defame others and abuse the ordinance of Christ. And though it be just in such a case, that he be materially dealt with as unjust accusers use to be in civil courts, yet this does not only flow from the consideration of such a persons being a formal accuser, but from the nature of the deed which is scandalous in such a measure, and that publicly, and therefore is to be restrained, whether the person take on him that formal consideration or not, lest yet, upon the matter, he continue publicly and importunately to press the pursuit. And we conceive, the imposing the title of accuser in such a case, or the making of it necessary, that one take on him that formal notion, is rather for conveniency to restrain men’s inordinateness and stop their mouths, and to add weight to the matter of the sentence if they fail, than as being simply necessary for making such a person to be accounted scandalous, if he come short.

t:
1. An unrighteous judge does condemn the cause of God Himself: For every righteous cause is his. 2. …It is a damnable sin not to relieve the innocent and imprisoned in their distress, when we have power…

3. It is a turning of the remedy into a double misery; and taking away the only help of oppressed innocency. What other defense has innocency, but Law and Justice? And when their refuge itself does fall upon them and oppress them, whither shall the righteous fly?

4. It subverts laws and government, and abuses it to destroy the ends which it is appointed for.

5. Thereby it turns human society into a state of misery, like the depredations of hostility.

6. It is a deliberate resolved sin, and not done in a passion by surprise: It is committed in that place, and in that form, as acts of greatest deliberation should be done: As if he should say, upon full disquisition, evidence and deliberation, I condemn this person, and his cause.

7. All this is done as in the Name of God, and by his own commission, by one that pretends to be his officer or minister, Rom. 3:3- 6. For the judgement is the Lord’s; 2 Chron. 19:8-10 & 19:5-7. And how great a wickedness is it thus to blaspheme, and to represent Him as Satan, an enemy to truth and righteousness, to his servants and Himself?…

8. It is sin against the fullest and frequentest prohibitions of God. Read over Ex. 23:1-3, etc.; Lev. 10:15; Dt. 1:16-17 & 16:18; Isa. 1:17, 20, 23; Dt. 24:17 & 27:19, ‘Cursed be he that perverts the judgement of the stranger, the fatherless and widow, and all the people shall say Amen’; Ezra 7:26; Ps. 33:5 & 37:28 & 72:2 & 94:15 & 106:3,30; Prov. 17:27 & 19:28 & 20:8 & 29:4 & 31:5; Eccl. 5:8; Isa. 5:7 & 10:2 & 56:1-2 & 59:14-15; Jer. 5:1 & 7:5 & 9:24; Eze. 18:8 & 45:9; Hos. 12:6; Amos 5:7,15,24 & 6:12; Mic. 3:9; Zech. 7:9 & 8:16; Gen. 18:19; Prov. 21:3,7,15. I cite not the words to avoid prolixity…

9. False judges cause the poor to appeal to God against them, and the cries of the afflicted shall not be forgotten, Lk. 18:5-8.

10. They call for God’s judgement upon themselves, and devolve the work into his hands… Ps. 9:7-9, ‘The Lord hath prepared his throne for judgement, and he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgement to the people in uprightness; he will be a refuge for the oppressed;’ Ps. 37:6, ‘He will bring forth righteousness as the light, and thy judgement as the noon day;’ Ps. 89:14, ‘Justice and judgement are the habitation of his throne;’ Ps. 103:6, ‘The Lord executeth righteousness and judgement for all that are oppressed;’ Ps. 146:7. In a word, the sentence of an unjust Judge is passed against his own soul, and he calls to God to condemn him righteously, who unrighteously condemned others. Of all men, he cannot stand in judgement, nor abide the righteous doom of Christ.
